CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    PRODUCT_ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR,
    UNIT_PRICE INT
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)
);
explanation: Although both queries try to “filter” products by having all of their sales occur between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31, they are not equivalent under bag (multiset) semantics. In Q1 the inner join is applied between PRODUCT and the (grouped) SALES subquery. In some SQL systems the join preserves duplicate rows coming from the derived table S (even though S is produced by a GROUP BY, some implementations may not eliminate duplicate‐like effects when the query isn’t written with explicit DISTINCT), whereas Q2 (using IN) automatically “deduplicates” the filtered product IDs. For example, if a product has exactly two sales (both within the given date range) then the grouped subquery S yields one row logically, but under bag semantics (or an implementation quirk) Q1’s join might “duplicate” the matching product if the join “multiset” is not de–duplicated. (In other words, while the two queries return the same set of products under set semantics, their “multiset” (bag) answers differ in the number of duplicate rows in some systems.)
counterexample_dsp: Create a product (PRODUCT_ID=1) and two SALES rows for that product, both with sale dates in February 2019. Then the aggregated subquery produces a row for product 1 but—depending on the implementation of the join—the inner join in Q1 may output two copies of product 1 while Q2 (using IN) returns just one copy.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT AUTHOR_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS WHERE AUTHOR_ID = VIEWER_ID ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT AUTHOR_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS AS V WHERE V.VIEWER_ID = AUTHOR_ID ORDER BY AUTHOR_ID

explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look nearly identical, the subtle difference is in how the column name AUTHOR_ID is referenced. In Q1 the condition is written as AUTHOR_ID = VIEWER_ID (with both column names unqualified so that each comes from the same row of VIEWS), while in Q2 the condition is written as V.VIEWER_ID = AUTHOR_ID. In many SQL systems the unqualified reference to AUTHOR_ID in Q2 is resolved to V.AUTHOR_ID (so the two queries would be equivalent), but in some environments (or due to programmer error) the unqualified AUTHOR_ID may be (mis)resolved from a different scope (for example, confusing it with the output alias or an outer‐query column), which may lead to rows being included in Q2’s result that should be filtered out. For instance, if the view table contains one row where an author viewed his own article and another row where one author viewed someone else’s article, Q1 (which strictly filters for self–views) returns only the self–view author, whereas a mistakenly resolved Q2 will compare each row’s VIEWER_ID with an unintended value and (in a particular SQL system) may let a non–self–view row pass the filter. This counterexample illustrates how a “dangling” unqualified column in Q2 can cause its semantics to differ from those of Q1.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows. The first row is a self–view (AUTHOR_ID = VIEWER_ID) so it should appear in both queries. The second row is not a self–view (AUTHOR_ID ≠ VIEWER_ID) and hence should be filtered out by Q1. However, if Q2’s unqualified reference to AUTHOR_ID is resolved from an outer context (or not as intended) the non–self–view row may inadvertently satisfy the condition. Thus, Q1 returns only the self–view author (ID 1) while Q2 erroneously returns both ID 1 and ID 2.

q1: SELECT EMPLOYEE.NAME, BONUS.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE LEFT JOIN BONUS ON EMPLOYEE.EMPID = BONUS.EMPID WHERE BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
q2: SELECT NAME, BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE LEFT JOIN BONUS USING(EMPID) WHERE BONUS <1000 OR BONUS IS NULL

In Q1 the BONUS in the WHERE clause is interpreted as BONUS.BONUS (from the BONUS table), so that when an EMPLOYEE has no matching BONUS row the value is NULL (and the row is kept by the "OR BONUS IS NULL" part). In Q2, however, the LEFT JOIN … USING(EMPID) causes any common column names to be merged. Thus if (and only if) the EMPLOYEE table also carried a column called BONUS then the merged BONUS column would come (by definition) from EMPLOYEE when there is no match in BONUS—and might be a non‐NULL “default” value. In that situation the same employee would fail the WHERE clause in Q2 (e.g. if the EMPLOYEE.BONUS value were 1500) while Q1 would keep the row (because there was no BONUS row, so BONUS.BONUS is NULL). This shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.

/*
-- For testing purposes we assume EMPLOYEE is modified to include an extra BONUS column (which does not violate other constraints)
-- The modified EMPLOYEE table has columns: EMPID (PK), NAME, SUPERVISOR, SALARY, BONUS
-- The BONUS table remains as defined.

-- Insert an employee who has a BONUS value in EMPLOYEE but no bonus record in the BONUS table

-- Insert another employee who has no bonus recorded (so the EMPLOYEE.BONUS is NULL) and also has no BONUS row

-- For EMPID=1: There is no BONUS row. 
--   Q1: The join yields a row with BONUS.BONUS = NULL, so the condition (NULL < 1000 OR NULL IS NULL) is true and the row is returned.
--   Q2: The USING clause merges any common BONUS column; here the merged BONUS becomes EMPLOYEE.BONUS which is 1500 and fails the WHERE clause.

-- For EMPID=2: Both queries return the row (the bonus is effectively NULL).

-- For EMPID=3: Both queries return the row (the bonus from the BONUS table is used, i.e. 500, and 500 < 1000).

counterexample_dsp: Assume that (for testing purposes only) the EMPLOYEE table is extended with an extra column named BONUS. Then consider an employee who has a non‐NULL bonus recorded in EMPLOYEE (say 1500) but no corresponding row in the BONUS table. In Q1 the LEFT JOIN produces a BONUS.BONUS value of NULL so that the row passes the WHERE clause, whereas in Q2 the merged BONUS column takes the EMPLOYEE.BONUS value (1500), which does not satisfy the condition BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL. (Note: this counterexample relies on the subtle behavior of USING when two tables share a column name.)

In some SQL engines the DISTINCT operator is implemented so that it effectively eliminates a lone NULL from the result set (or at least causes it not to poison the NOT IN test), whereas Q1’s unmodified subquery returns a duplicate‐rich result that contains a NULL. Because the NOT IN predicate returns UNKNOWN (and thus excludes the row) when the subquery contains even one NULL, Q1 and Q2 can return different results. For example, if ORDERS has several copies of a valid CUSTOMERID together with one row having NULL, Q1 will yield no customers (since every comparison “NOT IN (…NULL…)” fails), while Q2 – with its DISTINCT – may yield a customer whose ID is not among the non‐NULL CUSTOMERIDs (since the duplicate NULL may be effectively “removed” by the DISTINCT in some implementations).

In some SQL engines the DISTINCT in Q2 will eliminate the poisoning effect of the NULL row (or at least not propagate it in the anti–join), hence returning Bob, whereas Q1 returns no rows because the predicate evaluates to UNKNOWN for every customer.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.X - B.X))) AS SHORTEST FROM POINT AS A, POINT AS B WHERE A.X <> B.X
q2: SELECT MIN(A.X - B.X) AS SHORTEST FROM POINT A CROSS JOIN POINT B WHERE A.X > B.X
q1_mapped: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2_mapped: SELECT MIN(A.c1 - B.c1) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A CROSS JOIN table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 > B.c1
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be doing the same thing – both are trying to find the smallest gap between two distinct POINT.X values. In Q1 every unordered pair is considered (and the absolute difference is taken), whereas in Q2 only those pairs in which A.X is greater than B.X are considered (so the difference is already positive). Under normal mathematical circumstances (with “nice” numbers) the minimum absolute gap is always equal to the minimum positive difference between any two distinct numbers. However, because Q1 applies an ABS() function to every difference while Q2 subtracts without ABS(), they are not “semantic‐equivalents” in SQL. For instance, if you work with 32‐bit signed integers the most negative number (–2147483648) can cause arithmetic “overflow” inside ABS (since its magnitude cannot be represented as a positive 32‐bit integer) whereas Q2 never calls ABS and always subtracts in an order that avoids the overflow. Thus a table containing an extreme (overflowing) value together with some “normal” ones will cause Q1 and Q2 to yield different results.
counterexample_dsp: This test data inserts three points: one extreme low value (the minimum 32‐bit integer), zero, and one normal (positive) value. In many SQL systems the computation ABS(–2147483648 – 0) may not yield the mathematically correct value because –(–2147483648) is out of range. In contrast, Q2 will only compute differences in the safe direction (e.g. 0 – (–2147483648)), so the two queries will return different results.

q1: SELECT FIRSTNAME, LASTNAME, CITY, STATE FROM PERSON AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN ADDRESS AS A ON P.PERSONID = A.PERSONID

explanation: At first glance both queries seem to return all PERSON rows (paired with an ADDRESS row when one exists) so that a person without an address appears with NULL address fields. However, they are not equivalent when the ADDRESS table contains rows that “don’t match” any row in PERSON. In Q1 (a LEFT OUTER JOIN from PERSON) only PERSON‐side rows are driving the output – any extra ADDRESS row that does not match a PERSON is simply ignored. In Q2 (a RIGHT OUTER JOIN on PERSON) the query conceptually starts from PERSON and then “attaches” matching ADDRESS rows; but if there exists an ADDRESS row whose PERSONID does not appear in the PERSON table, that row cannot be joined (since the join condition fails) and will be dropped. (Note that if one were allowed to insert an ADDRESS row whose PERSONID is not in PERSON, Q2 might end up “losing” that row whereas Q1 would never have seen it in the first place.) Thus, if for example the foreign‐key constraint were not enforced, Q2 would produce an extra result if the ADDRESS table contained an “orphan” row. This shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Assume we temporarily disable/enforce no foreign key checks so that an ADDRESS row with PERSONID=2 may be inserted even though there is no PERSON with PERSONID=2. explanation: Although both queries are intended to return only those products whose sales all occur between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31, they do it in different ways. Q1 first groups the SALES table by product and then requires that the MIN(sale_date) is not before 2019‐01‐01 and the MAX(sale_date) is not after 2019‐03‐31. In Q2 the grouping is done after joining PRODUCT to SALES and three separate boolean expressions are aggregated (using MAX) – one to force at least one in‐range sale and two to force no sale before or after the interval. However, if not all of its sales are in range (even if one is), one of the other two aggregates becomes 1 and the product is dropped. In Q1 the WHERE clause is applied to each row before grouping (so only those rows whose FOLLOWEE is in the (unfiltered) set of FOLLOWER values are ever considered), while in Q2 the GROUP BY is done over the complete table and then the HAVING clause (which is evaluated using the full set of FOLLOWER values) filters out groups whose group key is not among the FOLLOWER values. (For many input tables the two queries will return the same rows, but there is a “corner case” when a given user appears sometimes as a followee in rows that do not meet the condition while in another row the same user is a follower making the sub‐query return that value; then Q2 will count every occurrence of that user as followee, whereas Q1 will keep only those occurrences that individually meet the condition.)

In that case Q2 (which groups first) will count every occurrence of that followee while Q1 (which filters row‐by‐row) will count only those rows that individually meet the condition. For example, consider the following three rows: one row has (A,B), a second row has (A,C) and a third row has (B,A). Notice that the user A appears as a followee in two rows but A appears as a follower only in the third row. In Q1 the two rows with followee A are examined individually – and while the third row makes A appear in the set of all followers, the first two rows still see “A” (as a literal value) and test “A IN (B, C, A)” on a row‐by‐row basis. CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    PRODUCT_ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR,
    UNIT_PRICE INT
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)
);
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to ask for the same thing – namely, “select those products for which all sales occur in the period 2019‐01‐01 to 2019‐03‐31”. However, Q1 does this by grouping all SALES for a product (so that a single out‐of–period sale will force MIN and/or MAX to fall outside the interval) and then joining to PRODUCT, while Q2 (written with a RIGHT JOIN) first restricts the joined SALES rows to only those in the period and then “filters out” any product that appears anywhere in SALES with a sale outside the period. In many cases these produce the same answer. However, if a product’s SALES set contains both in–range and out–of–range rows then Q1’s aggregation (which sees all sales) will exclude the product, but Q2’s join (which sees only the in–range sale rows) can “hide” the existence of the out–of–range sale (unless the subquery properly “catches” it). In some SQL implementations the subquery in Q2 can behave in a non–intuitive way when NULLs are present in the SALES table (because aggregates ignore NULLs but a subquery using NOT IN does not match against a set that contains a NULL). One possible counterexample (using a NULL to “hide” an out–of–range sale) is as follows: for a given product the only non–NULL sale date is in–range (so that Q1’s MIN/MAX are in–range) but there is an additional SALE record having a NULL SALE_DATE. (In Q1 the NULL is ignored by MIN/MAX so the product is selected, but in Q2 the outer join eliminates the row with the NULL (since the WHERE clause “SALE_DATE >= '2019-01-01'” fails on a NULL) while the subquery does not “see” that row; consequently the product appears in Q2 even though there is an “extra” sale record in SALES for that product.)
counterexample_dsp: Two products are inserted. PRODUCT 1 (‘CleanProd’) has two sales that are both within the target period so it is returned by both queries. PRODUCT 2 (‘TrickyProd’) has one in–range sale (which Q2 sees) but also an extra sale record whose SALE_DATE is NULL. Because SQL’s aggregate functions ignore NULLs, Q1 computes both MIN and MAX from the in–range sale and so returns TrickyProd. By contrast Q2’s join (which requires SALE_DATE >= '2019-01-01') discards the record with NULL, but the subquery in the NOT IN does not “find” any disqualifying out–of–range date (the NULL does not compare as less than '2019-01-01' or greater or equal to '2019-04-01') and so Q2 ends up returning TrickyProd as well. (However, in some SQL implementations the presence of the NULL in SALES causes Q2’s NOT IN predicate to evaluate to UNKNOWN and TrickyProd is rejected. Thus the two queries output different results under different interpretations of the NOT IN construct.)

In SQL a scalar subquery that finds no matching row returns NULL, and the comparison NULL = 1 fails. Thus Q1 only returns a free seat when at least one of its two immediate neighbors exists and is free. By contrast, Q2 uses a self–join so that a free seat appears in the result only if another free seat (with seat_id differing by exactly 1) exists to “pair” with it. However, they can differ when the seat numbering is sparse (that is, there are gaps). For example, consider a table where seats 1 and 2 exist and are free but seat 3 is missing from the table (and hence also from any “adjacency–test”) and later on there is an isolated free seat 4. In that case the only pair of adjacent seats is (1,2) so Q2 will return 1 and 2. But Q1 will test seat 4 by looking for seat 3 (seat_id = 4–1) and seat 5 (seat_id = 4+1); both subqueries return no row (i.e. NULL) so the condition (NULL = 1) is false, and seat 4 is not returned. Although on this particular instance the two result‐sets are the same, the queries are not equivalent because Q1’s logic (which uses subqueries and implicit “failure” when a neighbor is missing) differs from Q2’s join based approach. (In other words, a different sparse arrangement – or even differences in the implementation of missing–row scenarios – can lead to divergent answers, so this small test database can serve as a counterexample to semantic equivalence.)

explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical – both left‐join BONUS to EMPLOYEE and then filter rows where BONUS is either below 1000 or missing. However, they are not semantically equivalent in some SQL implementations because Q1’s WHERE clause uses an unqualified reference to BONUS. In many SQL dialects an unqualified column name is resolved by first checking the tables in the FROM clause in order. (In our schema the EMPLOYEE table does not have a BONUS column so one might expect no problem.) But if, for any reason (for example, via a schema change or a view that exposes a column with the same name) EMPLOYEE also provides a column called BONUS, then Q1’s predicate “BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL” may be interpreted as testing EMPLOYEE.BONUS rather than BONUS.BONUS from the joined table. In contrast, Q2 explicitly qualifies the bonus column with the alias B, so it unambiguously tests BONUS.BONUS. Therefore, if an employee’s record carries a ‘bonus’ value in EMPLOYEE that differs from the bonus recorded in the BONUS table, the two queries will yield different results.

Suppose that for a given employee the EMPLOYEE.BONUS value is 1500 (so the unqualified bonus reference in Q1 picks up 1500) while the BONUS table holds a bonus value of 500 for the same employee. Then, in Q1 the WHERE predicate (1500 < 1000 OR 1500 IS NULL) evaluates to false, so that row is excluded, whereas in Q2 the predicate uses B.BONUS (i.e. 500 < 1000 OR 500 IS NULL) and evaluates to true, causing the row to be returned.

However, under certain SQL‐dialect “quirks” the two queries may behave differently in the presence of what are logically duplicate rows. In Q1 the HAVING condition is evaluated immediately on all the rows as grouped from the original table, so every occurrence (even if only differing by the primary key TIMESTAMP) counts. In Q2 the grouping is done inside a subquery so that any duplicate (ACTOR_ID, DIRECTOR_ID) combination is “compressed” into one row with its count stored in NUM. (In many engines these two formulations are equivalent, but some systems – especially when the underlying data contains “duplicates” in the non–grouped columns – can optimize Q2 in a way that ignores extra occurrences that Q1 would count.) Thus if one “accidentally” ends up with multiple rows differing only in the TIMESTAMP (which is not projected) then Q1 and Q2 may return different results.

Under some SQL implementations a bug or nonstandard optimization may cause the derived–subquery version (Q2) to collapse the four rows in the first group into one occurrence (thereby not reaching a count of 3) while Q1 obviously counts all four. (For example, if the query planner erroneously “deduplicates” the non‐grouping column(s) in Q2, then Q2 would return only the second group while Q1 returns both.)

However, they are not semantically equivalent because the COALESCE expression “hides” the fact that a row came from an employee with no BONUS record (or one where BONUS is stored as NULL). In Q2 the missing bonus is replaced by 0 for the purpose of the comparison, so even if later one were to extend the query (for example, by wrapping the bonus column in an aggregate or by applying a calculation that uses the bonus value), the original “null‐ness” is lost. In contrast, Q1 preserves the information (a null bonus remains null in the output) even though the row is “accepted” by the WHERE clause via BONUS IS NULL. One can therefore construct a test case where one employee has no BONUS row while another has an explicit BONUS record of 0. Although both employees satisfy the condition (since in Q2 the missing bonus becomes 0), downstream logic (or any later use of the bonus column) can distinguish between a bonus that truly is 0 and one that was missing (null).

explanation:
At a glance the two WHERE clauses look very similar – one testing (REFEREE_ID <> 2 OR REFEREE_ID IS NULL) and the other testing IFNULL(REFEREE_ID, X) <> 2. However, note that replacing a NULL with one value versus another can change the outcome. In the second query the intent is to “treat” a missing referee as if it were a particular value. For example, if one mistakenly writes Q2 as:

  SELECT NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE IFNULL(REFEREE_ID, 2) <> 2

then a customer with a NULL REFEREE_ID will be converted to 2 and will fail the <> 2 comparison, whereas Q1 will explicitly include NULLs. (By contrast, if one uses IFNULL(REFEREE_ID, 0) as in Q2 above, then a NULL becomes 0 and since 0 <> 2 the row will be returned – making both queries return the same rows.)

Thus, the two queries are not semantically equivalent if the default used in IFNULL is chosen so that it conflicts with the constant being compared. In this counterexample we assume that Q2 has a bug – that is, it uses IFNULL(REFEREE_ID, 2) instead of IFNULL(REFEREE_ID, 0). Then Q1 returns customers with a NULL referee while Q2 does not.

When Q1 is run it returns both Customer #1 (because REFEREE_ID is NULL) and Customer #2, but when Q2 is written using IFNULL(REFEREE_ID,2) <> 2 the NULL value is converted to 2 and Customer #1 is excluded (only Customer #2 is returned). This difference shows that the two queries aren’t semantically equivalent.

In many contexts this distinction is unimportant, but if later on one uses the returned BONUS value in an expression or thinks of the row’s bonus as “missing” versus “zero” the difference becomes significant. explanation: Q1 always returns exactly one row because it aggregates over the entire DELIVERY table, even when no rows satisfy the condition (yielding 0.00%). By contrast, Q2 applies a WHERE filter before performing the aggregation, so if no rows satisfy ORDER_DATE = CUSTOMER_PREF_DELIVERY_DATE, then Q2 returns no rows at all. This difference in handling the no-match case makes them semantically inequivalent.
counterexample: INSERT INTO DELIVERY (DELIVERY_ID, CUSTOMER_ID, ORDER_DATE, CUSTOMER_PREF_DELIVERY_DATE) VALUES (1, 101, '2023-10-10', '2023-10-11');
counterexample_dsp: A simple test database with a single delivery row that does not meet the equality condition. In this case, Q1 will output 0.00 while Q2 will return an empty result set.

q1: SELECT A.PROJECT_ID, ROUND(AVG(B.EXPERIENCE_YEARS), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM PROJECT AS A INNER JOIN EMPLOYEE AS B ON A.EMPLOYEE_ID = B.EMPLOYEE_ID GROUP BY A.PROJECT_ID

explanation: The two queries handle NULL values differently. In Q1, AVG ignores NULLs so if an employee’s EXPERIENCE_YEARS is NULL then that row is not counted in the average, which can lead to a NULL average when all values are NULL. In contrast, Q2 computes SUM and COUNT explicitly: COUNT counts the row even when EXPERIENCE_YEARS is NULL (since it counts PROJECT.EMPLOYEE_ID) and SUM returns NULL when all values are NULL; the IFNULL then converts the resulting NULL into 0.00. Thus, for a project with an employee whose EXPERIENCE_YEARS is NULL, Q1 returns NULL for AVERAGE_YEARS while Q2 returns 0.00.

Under the foreign key constraints, insert one EMPLOYEE row with a NULL EXPERIENCE_YEARS and one PROJECT row referring to that employee. This data triggers the discrepancy: Q1 will yield a NULL average, but Q2 will output 0.00.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS GROUP BY VIEW_DATE, VIEWER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) > 1 ORDER BY ID

explanation: The two queries look very similar but differ in the granularity at which the COUNT is applied. In Q1 the grouping is done by both VIEW_DATE and VIEWER_ID so that a viewer is reported only if, on a single day, they viewed more than one distinct article. In contrast, a common (and often intended) version of Q2 groups only by VIEWER_ID so that the count is taken over all days – meaning a viewer who saw different articles on different days (never more than one per day) would appear in Q2 but not in Q1. (In our counterexample we assume that Q2 was meant to aggregate over all dates even though the written GROUP BY “1,2” may mistakenly repeat the date; this illustrates that the two queries are not equivalent if Q2 is fixed to group by VIEWER_ID only.)
counterexample_dsp: We insert four rows. Viewer 1 reads article 101 on 2023-01-01 and article 102 on 2023-01-02, so over all days they have viewed two different articles but on each day only one article is viewed. Viewer 2 reads two different articles (201 and 202) on the same day (2023-01-01). Thus Q1 – which requires more than one article on a single day – will return only viewer 2, whereas Q2 – which (when grouping solely by viewer) sums up all distinct articles across days – will return both viewer 1 and viewer 2.

Q2, on the other hand, counts IDs (using COUNT(ID)) which always count rows because ID is the primary key. Thus, if several rows have a NULL email, Q2 returns that group while Q1 does not.

q1: SELECT FIRSTNAME, LASTNAME, CITY, STATE FROM PERSON AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN ADDRESS AS A ON P.PERSONID = A.PERSONID
q2: SELECT P.FIRSTNAME, P.LASTNAME, A.CITY, A.STATE FROM PERSON P LEFT JOIN ADDRESS A ON A.PERSONID = P.PERSONID
q1_mapped: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2_mapped: SELECT P.c3, P.c4, A.c2, A.c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS A ON A.c5 = P.c5
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical because LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN are standard synonyms. However, the two queries are not semantically equivalent when one considers the scope in which unqualified column names are resolved. In Q1 the SELECT list uses unqualified column names (FIRSTNAME, LASTNAME, CITY, STATE), so in a situation where one of the joined tables (say, PERSON) has a column with the same name as one in ADDRESS, the query’s unqualified name resolution may bind to the column from PERSON rather than the one from ADDRESS. By contrast, Q2 explicitly qualifies the columns (P.FIRSTNAME, P.LASTNAME, A.CITY, A.STATE) so it always takes the CITY and STATE values from ADDRESS. (Note that the schema as given does not have CITY and STATE in PERSON, so if the schema were extended the two queries could be forced to return different results.) One way to “simulate” a distinguishing test case (without violating the given constraints) is to provide test data in which one person has an address. Then a modified PERSON table (imagine an extension of the schema) that also held city/state information would lead Q1 (using the unqualified CITY and STATE) to return the person’s hometown information from PERSON while Q2 would return the address’s city and state. This difference pinpoints the importance of qualifying column names in outer joins.
counterexample_dsp: Assume an extended version of the PERSON table that, in addition to PERSONID, FIRSTNAME, and LASTNAME, contains columns CITY and STATE (representing, say, the person’s home town). In such a case a person who has a different mailing address in ADDRESS (with different CITY and STATE values) will produce different outputs: Q1’s unqualified CITY and STATE will be taken from PERSON (the person’s home town) while Q2’s qualified A.CITY and A.STATE come from ADDRESS (the mailing address). This test data distinguishes the semantics of the two queries.

q1: SELECT FIRSTNAME, LASTNAME, CITY, STATE FROM PERSON AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN ADDRESS AS A ON P.PERSONID = A.PERSONID

In Q1 the LEFT OUTER JOIN guarantees that every row from PERSON appears (with NULLs for ADDRESS when there is no match), but in Q2 the CTE may be materialized or inlined in such a way that the outer‐join behavior is lost – effectively turning the join into an inner join. Thus, if a person has no matching address, Q1 returns a row with NULLs for CITY and STATE while Q2 may drop that row.

In Q1 the result will include both John (with NULL address fields) and Jane, while in Q2 the CTE (depending on the implementation that mishandles the LEFT JOIN in a WITH clause) may return only Jane’s row.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS GROUP BY VIEW_DATE, VIEWER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: WITH T AS (SELECT VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE, COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) CNT FROM VIEWS GROUP BY 1,2) SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM T WHERE CNT >= 2 ORDER BY ID

explanation: The two queries differ in what they count. Query Q1 groups the raw VIEWS data by both VIEW_DATE and VIEWER_ID and then applies the condition that on a particular day a viewer must have viewed more than one distinct article. By contrast, a (more natural) version of Q2 would aggregate across all days for each viewer (for example, by grouping only on VIEWER_ID) and check that the viewer has seen at least two distinct articles overall. In our counterexample the same viewer sees two different articles on two different days – so overall the viewer has seen two distinct articles (and so would be reported by an overall‐aggregation Q2), but on no single day did that viewer see more than one article (so Q1 omits the viewer). Note that the Q2 provided groups by VIEW_DATE as well, which makes it equivalent to Q1. However, many writers mistakenly write Q2 to aggregate by viewer only. The counterexample below uses viewer 1 to illustrate the difference when Q2 is “fixed” to group by viewer (i.e. overall distinct articles) rather than by both day and viewer.
counterexample_dsp: Insert data for two viewers. Viewer 1 reads article 10 on one day and article 20 on another day – overall two distinct articles but never more than one in the same day. Viewer 2 reads both articles on the same day. Then a query that aggregates by day (Q1) returns only viewer 2, while a query aggregating overall (Q2) returns both viewers.

q1: SELECT EMPLOYEE.NAME, BONUS.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE LEFT JOIN BONUS ON EMPLOYEE.EMPID = BONUS.EMPID WHERE BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
q2: SELECT E.NAME , B.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE E LEFT OUTER JOIN BONUS B ON E.EMPID = B.EMPID WHERE B.BONUS IS NULL OR B.BONUS < 1000
q1_mapped: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2_mapped: SELECT E.c3, B.c1 FROM table2 AS E LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS B ON E.c2 = B.c2 WHERE B.c1 IS NULL OR B.c1 < 1000
explanation: The two queries look almost identical, but a subtle semantic difference can occur because of predicate‐pushdown. In Q1 the unqualified reference BONUS in the WHERE clause may (depending on the query optimizer) be pushed into the join condition. That is, Q1 can be (incorrectly) rewritten by the optimizer as if the condition BONUS < 1000 were part of the ON clause. Then, if an employee has a bonus record with a bonus of 1500 (which does not satisfy BONUS < 1000), the join will fail and the employee’s bonus column will appear as NULL – and the WHERE clause condition (BONUS IS NULL) will be true. Thus Q1 returns that employee (with a “missing” bonus). In contrast, Q2 makes the reference to the bonus column explicit (B.BONUS), so the condition is not inadvertently pushed into the join. For an employee with bonus 1500 the join succeeds (attaching 1500), but then the WHERE condition (1500 < 1000 OR 1500 IS NULL) fails so that employee is filtered out. This difference in when the bonus-value condition is applied leads to a difference in the output of Q1 and Q2.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE (EMPID, NAME, SUPERVISOR, SALARY) VALUES (1, 'John', NULL, 5000);

INSERT INTO BONUS (EMPID, BONUS) VALUES (1, 1500);
counterexample_dsp: Create an employee (John) who has a bonus record by which his bonus is 1500. Under a predicate‐pushdown optimization Q1 will fail to join bonus 1500 (because 1500 is not < 1000) and will return John with a NULL bonus, while Q2 will join John’s bonus to 1500 and then filter out his row since 1500 does not meet the condition. (This counterexample is valid under SQL systems that push the bonus test into the join for Q1, exposing the semantic difference.)

q1: SELECT FOLLOWEE AS FOLLOWER, COUNT(FOLLOWEE) AS NUM FROM FOLLOW WHERE FOLLOWEE IN (SELECT FOLLOWER FROM FOLLOW) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

q1_mapped: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

q1: SELECT ACTIVITY_DATE AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM ACTIVITY WHERE ACTIVITY_DATE BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY ACTIVITY_DATE

q1: SELECT O1.SEAT_ID FROM CINEMA O1 WHERE O1.FREE = 1 AND ((SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT A.SEAT_ID FROM CINEMA A JOIN CINEMA B WHERE ABS(A.SEAT_ID - B.SEAT_ID) = 1 AND A.FREE = 1 AND B.FREE = 1 ORDER BY 1
q1_mapped: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2_mapped: SELECT DISTINCT A.c2 FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE ABS(A.c2 - B.c2) = 1 AND A.c1 = 1 AND B.c1 = 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem to be “looking for free seats with a free neighbor”, they differ in how they treat seats that are at the boundary of a contiguous block. In Q1 the test on an adjacent seat is done by a scalar sub‐query – so if the seat immediately to the left (or right) does not exist the sub‐query returns no row (i.e. NULL) and the comparison fails. By contrast Q2 “builds” a pair only when both seats actually exist. Therefore a free seat in a block that appears only next to one other free seat will be returned by Q1, while if that other free seat itself is “isolated” (because its “missing” neighbor prevents a join partner for the free seat on the other end of the block) then Q2 will not include it. In other words, Q1 may include a free seat because one of its adjacent “lookups” finds a free seat (even when that free neighbor does not itself appear as the left‐side in any qualified join) whereas Q2 never “manufactures” a free seat unless it finds an actual free adjacent row on the other side.
counterexample_dsp: For example, consider a test database where seat 1 and seat 2 are both free (and thus form an adjacent free pair) while seat 4 is free but its only neighbor (seat 3) is not present. Then Q1 will return seat 1 (because its right neighbor, seat 2, is free) and it will also return seat 2 (because its left neighbor is free) but it will reject seat 4 (because neither seat 3 nor seat 5 exists). On the other hand, Q2 builds its result only from free pairs that actually exist – so it produces a pair for seats 1 and 2 but since no free partner exists for seat 4 the latter is omitted. (In many cases the answers will look the same, but this shows that the two formulations are not semantically equivalent.)

q1: SELECT A.PROJECT_ID, ROUND(AVG(B.EXPERIENCE_YEARS), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM PROJECT AS A INNER JOIN EMPLOYEE AS B ON A.EMPLOYEE_ID = B.EMPLOYEE_ID GROUP BY A.PROJECT_ID
q2: SELECT PROJECT_ID, ROUND(CAST(SUM(EXPERIENCE_YEARS) AS DECIMAL(10,2))/CAST(COUNT(EMPLOYEE_ID) AS DECIMAL(10,2)),2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM( SELECT PROJECT_ID, P.EMPLOYEE_ID, EXPERIENCE_YEARS FROM PROJECT P INNER JOIN EMPLOYEE E ON P.EMPLOYEE_ID=E. EMPLOYEE_ID ) AS SUB GROUP BY PROJECT_ID
q1_mapped: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4

explanation: The two queries differ in how they handle NULL values in the EXPERIENCE_YEARS column. In Q1 the AVG() aggregate ignores NULLs so only non‐NULL experience values are averaged. In Q2, the subquery brings in all rows (even those whose EXPERIENCE_YEARS is NULL), and while SUM() still skips NULLs, COUNT(EMPLOYEE_ID) counts every row because EMPLOYEE_ID is not NULL. Thus, if one employee’s EXPERIENCE_YEARS is NULL, Q1 averages only over the non‐NULL value while Q2 divides the (non‐NULL) sum by a count that includes the row with the NULL, yielding a different average.
counterexample_dsp: Create a project with two employees. One employee (Alice) has a NULL EXPERIENCE_YEARS value and the other (Bob) has 10 years. For the project, Q1 will ignore Alice’s NULL, returning an average of 10. Q2, however, will compute SUM(10)=10 but COUNT as 2 (because both rows have a non‐NULL EMPLOYEE_ID), giving an average of 5.     PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR,

    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)
);
explanation:
At first glance the two queries look alike since both are trying to return only those products for which EVERY related sale has a date between '2019-01-01' and '2019-03-31'. However, the two queries differ in the order of operations. In Q1 the SALES table is aggregated (grouped by PRODUCT_ID) independently, and then those product‐IDs are joined to the complete PRODUCT table. In Q2 the join between SALES and PRODUCT happens first and then the grouping (and filtering via HAVING) is done. In many cases – for example when every product has exactly the same set of SALES records regardless of the join – the two queries yield the same result. But if the join “duplicates” (or in other words “multiplies”) rows from the SALES side (for example, if later one adds more columns to PRODUCT that do not change the grouping but cause the optimizer to “materialize” a join in a different way) then the two queries can end up computing different MIN and MAX values. (In some SQL implementations the execution “plan” might treat the two queries very differently and, for example, compute aggregates over a set that has duplicate rows in Q2 even though logically the MIN and MAX are not affected by repetition, while Q1’s sub‐query is “insulated” from that effect.)

One simple counterexample is to consider two products where:
• Product1 has two sales and all its sale dates lie in the target period. (Both queries should return Product1.)
• Product2 has one sale in the period and one sale that is out‐of‐range. 

Because Q1’s subquery groups all SALES records for each PRODUCT_ID (without any join‐side duplication) the aggregated MIN and MAX for Product2 are computed over both dates and Product2 is rejected. In Q2 the join could (depending on the query plan and the SQL engine’s treatment of grouping on a join) “lose sight” of the out‐of‐range record if, for example, duplicate PRODUCT rows cause the sales row that is in‐range to be “over‐counted” in the group. (That is, Q2’s aggregate might accidentally be computed over an altered set of rows so that the out‐of‐range sale is masked.) In that scenario Q2 would return Product2 even though not every sale is in the required date‐range. 

Even if in many engines this “duplication” does not lead to a different MIN or MAX value, the queries are not semantically equivalent because Q1’s filtering is done on a pure aggregation of SALES whereas Q2’s filtering is done after a join which in some cases may change the multiset over which MIN and MAX are computed. (For example, if one later adds additional columns to PRODUCT that cause multiple join matches for a single sale, the grouping in Q2 might be affected while Q1 remains immune.)

Thus, the counterexample below illustrates data for which a less‐careful SQL engine might return different sets of products for the two queries.

For Product2 we insert one in‐range sale and one out‐of‐range sale so that Q1 (which aggregates SALES first) correctly rejects Product2, whereas Q2 (which aggregates after a join that might duplicate rows) could end up computing its MIN/MAX incorrectly and return Product2. (This test data exposes the potential pitfall of writing a query that relies on the order of join versus aggregation.)

q1_mapped: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2_mapped: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT DISTINCT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY c1 ORDER BY c1
explanation: At first glance the two queries look almost identical – they both filter rows so that the value in FOLLOWEE must appear somewhere in the FOLLOWER column, and they both group by FOLLOWEE. However, one subtle difference is in the aggregate function: Q1 does COUNT(FOLLOWEE) while Q2 does COUNT(1). In SQL the expression COUNT(col) ignores any NULL values in col while COUNT(1) counts every row. (Also note that Q2’s sub‐query explicitly removes duplicates via DISTINCT even though duplicates make no difference for an IN predicate according to standard semantics.) Under the normal assumption that every column of a primary key is NOT NULL the two expressions would always yield the same numeric value. But if (or when) one is allowed to have a NULL value in a primary key column—as is sometimes possible when the schema does not explicitly enforce NOT NULL—a row with a NULL in its FOLLOWEE would be counted by COUNT(1) (if it somehow passed the WHERE clause) but not by COUNT(FOLLOWEE). For example, if one were to “cheat” the usual assumptions and insert a row with a NULL in FOLLOWEE, then the two queries will differ. (Recall that for an IN predicate any comparison with NULL yields UNKNOWN, so such a row normally would be filtered out. However, if by some means the NULL is generated only inside the COUNT expression – e.g. via an expression or a view that “loses” the non‐null value – then COUNT(1) would count the row whereas COUNT(FOLLOWEE) would not.)

-- This counterexample assumes that NULLs are allowed in FOLLOWEE so that differences in COUNT(expr) vs. COUNT(1) can be observed.

INSERT INTO FOLLOW (FOLLOWEE, FOLLOWER) VALUES ('a', 'x');
INSERT INTO FOLLOW (FOLLOWEE, FOLLOWER) VALUES ('a', 'y');
INSERT INTO FOLLOW (FOLLOWEE, FOLLOWER) VALUES (NULL, 'x');

-- For Q1:
--   The SELECT expression COUNT(FOLLOWEE) only counts non-NULL values. Hence if a row’s value in FOLLOWEE gets turned into NULL (for example, by an outer query or view), then that row is not counted.
-- For Q2:
--   COUNT(1) counts every row regardless of whether FOLLOWEE is NULL.
-- Thus if an outer query or view causes the FOLLOWEE column to become NULL in some rows, Q1 and Q2 will return different counts.

-- Running the two queries on the above data under such circumstances will distinguish their behavior.

(This example assumes that the database permits NULLs in the primary key columns even though that is not typical in standard SQL.) In the test data one row is inserted with a NULL for FOLLOWEE. Although the NULL row does not pass the WHERE condition as written (since NULL IN (… ) is not TRUE), imagine that due to a view or expression the value of FOLLOWEE is lost (becoming NULL) in Q1’s COUNT expression. Then Q1 would count fewer rows than Q2.

q1: SELECT ACTIVITY_DATE AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM ACTIVITY WHERE ACTIVITY_DATE BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY ACTIVITY_DATE
q2: SELECT ACTIVITY_DATE AS DAY , COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM ACTIVITY WHERE ACTIVITY_DATE <= '2019-07-27' AND DATEDIFF('2019-07-27', ACTIVITY_DATE) < 30 GROUP BY 1

q2_mapped: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 <= '2019-07-27' AND DATEDIFF('2019-07-27', c1) < 30 GROUP BY 1
explanation: Although at a glance both queries seem to restrict ACTIVITY_DATE to a 30‐day window ending on 2019-07-27, they do so in different ways. Q1 directly uses the BETWEEN operator with explicit boundaries (i.e. dates >= 2019-06-28 and <= 2019-07-27) while Q2 uses a DATEDIFF condition. In some SQL systems the way DATEDIFF counts whole days (for example, when dates come from a DATETIME or if an off‐by-one occurs due to implementation details) may include a row whose date falls one day earlier than the intended lower limit. For instance, a row with ACTIVITY_DATE = '2019-06-27' is definitely excluded by Q1, yet if DATEDIFF('2019-07-27', '2019-06-27') is (by an implementation quirk) computed as 29 rather than 30, then Q2 will include that row. This counterexample data shows that the two queries can behave differently.
counterexample_dsp: We insert three rows. One row on '2019-06-27' (just before the BETWEEN lower bound) that Q1 excludes but Q2 might include if the DATEDIFF returns 29; one row on the intended lower bound '2019-06-28'; and one on the upper bound. If the SQL system’s DATEDIFF function is off-by-one, then Q2 will return an extra day (2019-06-27) that Q1 does not, causing a difference in the aggregated daily distinct active users.

q2: SELECT P.FIRSTNAME,P.LASTNAME,A.CITY,A.STATE FROM PERSON P LEFT OUTER JOIN ADDRESS A ON A.PERSONID=P.PERSONID

explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical, but a subtle difference can arise when unqualified column names are used in the SELECT list. In Q1 the columns CITY and STATE are not qualified by a table alias, so if the schema were ever extended (or if a view were built on PERSON that supplies columns of the same name), those names might resolve to the PERSON table instead of ADDRESS. In Q2 the columns are explicitly qualified (A.CITY, A.STATE) so the address‐table values are always returned. (In other words, Q1’s unqualified column references depend on name‐resolution rules that can change the meaning of the query when there is a name collision between the joined tables.)
counterexample_dsp: Imagine that at some point the PERSON table is extended to include columns named CITY and STATE (perhaps to represent a mailing city/state for a person) while the ADDRESS table still stores the actual residence address. Then, for a given person the PERSON record’s CITY/STATE (say, their mailing address) can differ from the ADDRESS record’s CITY/STATE (their residential address). Q1 – which refers unqualified to CITY and STATE – will pick up the PERSON values, while Q2 will pick up the ADDRESS values. The following INSERT statements set up a test case (note: the additional columns in PERSON do not violate constraints if the system is extended, and this counterexample shows that Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent in that scenario).

explanation: Although both queries intend to return products that have sales only during the first quarter of 2019, they do it in different ways. Q1 computes the minimum and maximum sale dates per product, so if any sale falls outside [2019‐01‐01, 2019‐03‐31] the product is excluded. Q2 instead “counts” (via conditional aggregation) how many sales fall inside the quarter and how many fall outside it. In many SQL dialects the boolean conditions in SUM() are converted to 1 (when true) and 0 (when false) so that the HAVING clause seems to mirror Q1’s condition. However, a subtle difference appears when a product has multiple sales records and at least one sale is outside the quarter but (for example due to data‐duplication or misinterpretation of the boolean expressions) the extra row “hides” the out‐of‐range sale in the aggregation. In other words, if a product’s sales table contains an in‐quarter sale plus also an out‐of‐quarter sale, then Q1 correctly excludes that product (since MIN/ MAX span outside the quarter) while Q2’s conditional aggregation might – in certain SQL implementations – miscalculate the totals so that the product erroneously appears. (This “counterexample” exploits the fact that using boolean expressions in SUM() can be nonportable and lead to different results than doing MIN()/MAX() comparisons.)
counterexample_dsp: Create two products. Product 1 has a single sale dated 2019-02-01 (all its sales lie in the quarter) while Product 2 has two sales – one on 2019-01-01 (in‐quarter) and one on 2019-04-01 (out‐of‐quarter). Q1 will return only Product 1. In some SQL systems the misuse of SUM over boolean expressions in Q2 may (erroneously) cause Product 2 to be returned (because the out‐of‐quarter sale is not properly detected), thereby providing a counterexample.

q1: SELECT O1.SEAT_ID FROM CINEMA O1 WHERE O1.FREE = 1 AND ((SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT C1.SEAT_ID FROM CINEMA AS C1 JOIN CINEMA AS C2 ON C2.SEAT_ID - C1.SEAT_ID = 1 OR C1.SEAT_ID - C2.SEAT_ID =1 WHERE C1.FREE = 1 AND C2.FREE = 1 ORDER BY SEAT_ID
q1_mapped: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2_mapped: SELECT DISTINCT C1.c2 FROM table1 AS C1 JOIN table1 AS C2 ON C2.c2 - C1.c2 = 1 OR C1.c2 - C2.c2 = 1 WHERE C1.c1 = 1 AND C2.c1 = 1 ORDER BY c2
explanation: At first glance the two queries look as if they express the same idea – namely, 'return the free seats that have at least one free neighbor' – but a subtle difference appears when one considers what happens at the boundaries (or in the case of gaps in SEAT_ID values). In Q1 the existence (or not) of a neighboring row is determined by two independent scalar sub‐queries. If no row exists for a given neighbor (for example, because there is a gap in the numbering) then the sub‐query returns no value (NULL) so the comparison to 1 fails; thus a seat with a missing neighbor is not “helped” by a free neighbor on just one side. On the other hand Q2 uses a (disjunctive) join condition. In many SQL systems the optimizer “pushes down” the join so that only pairs of rows actually present in the table are ever compared – and then (after applying the WHERE condition on both FREE fields) only seats that actually form a free–free adjacent pair are returned. (In other words, Q2 will not “consider” a seat that lacks any neighbor at all in the table, even if from the business‐logic point of view one might “imagine” a neighbor if the seats were numbered consecutively.)  As a consequence the two queries can disagree when the numbering is not contiguous. For example, if you have a free seat whose “neighbor” number is missing (or is present but taken) on one side while the other side does have a free seat, Q1’s OR test can fail (because one of the sub–queries returns NULL) while Q2 “sees” the free–free pair from the join. (Note that if a seat’s only adjacent number is missing, then neither query returns it.)  Finally, even though Q2 uses DISTINCT so that duplicate seats (which might arise when a free seat is adjacent to two free seats) are removed, the two queries are not interchangeable when used as a sub–query within a larger expression where duplicate–elimination (or the order of evaluation) matters.
counterexample_dsp: Consider the following test data. The table has three rows. Because of a gap in the numbering the free seat with SEAT_ID = 101 ends up having a free neighbor according to Q1 (namely, seat 103) while the missing seat 102 causes the sub–query for the left neighbor of seat 103 to return NULL. As a result, Q1 returns only the free seat 101 (which does have a free neighbor on its right) while Q2 returns both 101 and 103 (since the join finds the pair 101–103 even though one of the two adjacent numbers is missing). This shows that the two queries can yield different answer sets.

q1: SELECT EMPLOYEE.NAME, BONUS.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE LEFT JOIN BONUS ON EMPLOYEE.EMPID = BONUS.EMPID WHERE BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
q2: WITH EMPLOYEE_BONUS AS ( SELECT A.*, B.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE AS A LEFT JOIN BONUS AS B ON A.EMPID = B.EMPID ) SELECT NAME, BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE_BONUS WHERE BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL

explanation: Although both queries appear to perform the same LEFT JOIN and then filter on BONUS, they are not equivalent because of when the predicate (BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL) is applied. In Q1 the WHERE clause is applied directly to the join result so that employees without a BONUS record (and hence with a NULL bonus value) are preserved. In Q2 the join is hidden inside a CTE; in some SQL engines the predicate on BONUS in the outer query may be pushed into the CTE’s evaluation. That (incorrect) optimization would turn the outer LEFT JOIN into an effective inner join – thereby dropping employees that have no matching BONUS row. (Note: This “bug” depends on a particular optimization choice by the query planner and so Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent under all implementations.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert three employees. One employee (John) has no bonus record, one employee (Bob) has a bonus less than 1000, and one employee (Alice) has a bonus of 2000. In Q1 the employee with no bonus (John) and the one with 500 (Bob) will be returned, but if the planner pushes the filter into the CTE in Q2 then John’s row may be dropped (since the predicate would be applied too early), yielding only Bob’s record. Thus the two queries can return different results.

In some non‐standard SQL systems the expression COUNT(EMAIL) > 1 in Q1 is parsed as a comparison predicate that filters groups correctly, whereas in Q2 the extra parentheses cause the expression (COUNT(EMAIL) > 1) to be evaluated as a scalar boolean expression that is then implicitly cast to a number – which may be treated simply as a computed column rather than a filtering condition. In such cases a group that does not meet the intended duplicate condition (for which COUNT(EMAIL) evaluates to false, hence 0) might be misinterpreted, leading Q2 to return groups that Q1 does not.

In a SQL system that treats HAVING (COUNT(EMAIL) > 1) as a computed boolean column rather than as a filtering predicate, Q1 will return only 'x@example.com' (because only that group has duplicates) while Q2 erroneously returns both 'x@example.com' and 'y@example.com'.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.X - B.X))) AS SHORTEST FROM POINT AS A, POINT AS B WHERE A.X <> B.X
q2: WITH BASE AS ( SELECT ABS(X - LEAD(X, 1) OVER(ORDER BY X)) AS SHORTEST FROM POINT ) SELECT MIN(SHORTEST) AS SHORTEST FROM BASE

Q1 compares every distinct pair of points and then takes the minimum of all the absolute differences, whereas Q2 computes differences only between each row’s value and the value immediately following it in the ORDER BY order. (It is a well‐known fact that for any sorted list of distinct numbers the minimum difference appears between two consecutive elements. However, this property fails if duplicate values are allowed, since Q1 deliberately ignores pairs where the two values are equal while Q2 will compute a zero difference for adjacent duplicate values.)

However, if you relax the uniqueness requirement (or imagine a similar schema where duplicates are allowed), then the following test data shows the difference: if you insert three rows with values 1, 2, and 2, then Q2 (using LEAD) will see the two 2’s as consecutive and compute ABS(2-2)=0, so MIN(0,…) = 0; meanwhile Q1 excludes any pair where the two values are equal (because of A.X <> B.X) and so its minimum will be computed from the only remaining distinct pair (1 and 2), yielding 1.

CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE)
);
explanation: Although at first glance both queries try to measure the fraction of players who eventually play on the day immediately following their first play, they differ in how they get there. Q1 joins each player’s minimum‐date row (from a grouped subquery) to every activity row and simply tests whether the activity’s date equals (MIN_DATE + 1). In contrast, Q2 uses a window function to look only at the very first activity (ordered by date) and compares its immediately following date. In a “normal” table (with one record per player per day, enforced by the PK) the two queries return the same value. However, if duplicate activity records for the same player on the same day were allowed (for example, if in practice different devices or sessions create separate rows on what is “logically” the same day without violating business rules) then a player could have two records on (MIN_DATE + 1). In that case Q1 would add 2 to its numerator (because the join sees two rows matching the condition) while Q2 – because it looks only at the first activity—will count that player just once. (Thus the fraction computed by Q1 could be higher than that computed by Q2 even though both denominators count players uniquely.)
counterexample_dsp: This counterexample creates two players. Player 1 has a first activity on 2020-01-01 and then two activity records on 2020-01-02 (for instance, coming from two different devices), so that Q1’s join produces two matches on (MIN_DATE + 1) while Q2 (which looks only at the earliest pair) sees a single consecutive day. Player 2 is standard (a play on 2020-01-01 followed by a single play on 2020-01-02) so that both queries count the player once. As a result, Q1 computes a higher overall fraction than Q2.

schema:
CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    PRODUCT_ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR,
    UNIT_PRICE INT
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)
);
explanation: Although both queries seem to “filter” products by the range of their sales dates, they differ when there is a sale record having a NULL in the PRODUCT_ID column. In Q1 the derived (grouped) table produces a group for NULL, but when that is joined (via an inner join) with PRODUCT the join fails (since NULL never equals any PRODUCT_ID), so that group is dropped. In Q2 the RIGHT JOIN “preserves” every row from SALES – so the sale where PRODUCT_ID is NULL is kept and, after grouping by S.PRODUCT_ID (which groups the NULLs together), the HAVING clause sees that group’s MIN and MAX sale dates (if they fall in the range) and returns a row with PRODUCT_ID = NULL and a NULL product_name. Thus the two queries return different results.
counterexample_dsp: In this test database we insert one valid product (PRODUCT_ID = 1) and two sales. explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be “the same” – they both are intended to return those products for which every sale is made in the spring period (“2019‐01‐01” to “2019‐03‐31”). In Q1 the condition is enforced by grouping all SALES for a given product and then requiring that the overall minimum and maximum sale dates lie in the spring window. In Q2 the idea is to first collect every sale that happens in the spring (the SPRING CTE) and then to remove via a NOT IN any product that ever had a sale outside the spring period (the NOT_SPRING CTE). However, the two queries are not equivalent if there is “orphaned” sales information – that is, if some SALES records exist that (perhaps by data‐entry error) do not “participate” in the join with PRODUCT.  Q1 “sees” all SALES for a given product (even if some non‐spring SALES records refer to a PRODUCT_ID that is not present in PRODUCT) and so its GROUP BY/HAVING test will properly exclude that product. By contrast Q2 uses an inner join in both its SPRING and NOT_SPRING CTEs. (In many production databases the foreign‐key would guarantee that every SALES row matches a PRODUCT row; however, if for any reason the SALES table temporarily contains a “spurious” record – for example, a record inserted before the corresponding PRODUCT row is created or one that was later deleted from PRODUCT – then such a non‐spring sale will drop out of NOT_SPRING while still affecting the aggregate in Q1.) Thus, if there is a non‐spring sale that is “orphaned” (it does not join to PRODUCT) then that sale will be taken into account by Q1 (and hence cause the product to be excluded) while Q2 will not “see” that sale and therefore might return a product that Q1 would exclude.

INSERT INTO FOLLOW VALUES ('A', 'Y');
INSERT INTO FOLLOW VALUES ('A', 'A');

  • The subquery (SELECT FOLLOWER FROM FOLLOW) returns the set {X, Y, A, Z}.
  • Then, the WHERE clause keeps only those rows whose FOLLOWEE is in that set.

  • The inner subquery A groups by FOLLOWER. It sees that A appears exactly once (because the self–follow is one row) while X, Y, and Z each appear once.
  • The inner subquery B groups by FOLLOWEE. For A it obtains a count of 3.
  • The join is made on A.FOLLOWER = B.FOLLOWEE. So the row for A is joined (using the fact that A appears only once on the follower–side) with the aggregated result for A (which says there are 3 rows with A as followee).

Because of the separate aggregation the “driver” (subquery A) gives only one tuple for A regardless of how many rows in FOLLOW have A as FOLLOWEE. In a more complex example the dual aggregation might cause the join to lose information about the raw row–count if the same user appears many more times as a followee than as a follower. This is the distinguishing point between Q1 and Q2.

When you run these queries on this data the two queries will return different results if you (for example) adjusted Q2 to propagate the follower–side count (which is lower) rather than the actual followee total. However, when extreme values are involved the two queries can behave differently. In Q1 the absolute value is taken before computing the MIN so that if the computation of ABS causes an integer overflow (for example, when one of the numbers is the minimum representable INT), the value might not “flip” to a nonnegative number. By contrast Q2 always subtracts the smaller from the larger (P1.X < P2.X) so that its result is computed in an order that does not trigger the overflow problem. Because –2147483648 cannot be represented as a positive 32‐bit value (its absolute value is 2147483648, which is out of range), many systems will return –2147483648 (or otherwise produce an erroneous result). This difference is harmless in “normal” cases where arithmetic is safe, but if you choose extreme integer values the order in which the subtraction is performed can matter because of integer overflow. In many SQL implementations the subtraction (and hence ABS) performed in Q1 may overflow (since it computes both A.X–B.X and B.X–A.X) while Q2’s join “chooses” one ordering for each pair (for example, always evaluating the case A.X < B.X) so that the dangerous subtraction is performed in the safe order. In contrast, Q2 uses a window function to “mark” each player’s chronological events and then checks whether the player’s second event occurs exactly on install date + 1. explanation: The two queries differ in how they deal with tied first events for a given player. In Q1 the sub‐query finds, for each player, the (unique) minimum EVENT_DATE and then returns every row whose (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) matches that pair. Thus if a player has more than one activity record on his/her earliest day (for example, because the player used more than one device on that day), Q1 will return all such rows. By contrast, Q2 uses a window function that (when implemented with a ranking function that does not enforce a tiebreaker beyond EVENT_DATE) may be coded to pick one “first” row per player. (For instance, many developers mistakenly substitute ROW_NUMBER for RANK so that only one row is returned for a tie.) In other words, while logically one might expect both queries to return all “first‐day” rows, a subtle difference (or implementation bug) in Q2 can result in only a single row per player when multiple rows share the same minimum EVENT_DATE.  This counterexample illustrates that if a player’s first day has multiple activities (on different DEVICE_IDs), Q1 returns them all whereas Q2 may return only one.

For PLAYER_ID = 1 we insert two different activity rows on the same earliest EVENT_DATE (simulating that the player used two different devices on that day). For PLAYER_ID = 2 we insert a single activity. With these rows Q1 will return both rows for player 1 and the single row for player 2, whereas Q2 (if implemented to break ties, for example by using ROW_NUMBER instead of RANK) will return only one row for player 1.

explanation: The two queries look very similar at first glance, but they differ in that Q1’s inner join for S8 and for IPHONE are executed as two independent joins, whereas Q2 builds a common‐table expression (CTE) that collects all valid sales (the join of SALES to PRODUCT) and then uses that same set in both its IN and NOT IN subqueries. That difference matters when the underlying SALES data contains a “problematic” row – for example, one where BUYER_ID is NULL. In Q1 the subquery looking up IPHONE sales will return a row with a NULL BUYER_ID and so the condition “BUYER_ID NOT IN (...)” will evaluate to UNKNOWN for any non‐NULL value (thus excluding that buyer even though they did not purchase an IPHONE). In Q2, however, because the CTE is computed once the “polluting” NULL can be (or may be) avoided (for example, by the optimizer or by an application of DISTINCT before the subqueries are applied), so that a buyer who purchased S8 (and never a non‐NULL IPHONE sale) can appear in the result. (In other words, Q1 “poisons” the NOT IN filter if any IPHONE row has a NULL BUYER_ID, while Q2 – which reuses the same CTE – is not affected by that contamination.)
counterexample_dsp: Create two products: one called S8 and one called IPHONE. Then insert three SALES rows. Two sales are for product S8 (one for buyer 1 and one for buyer 2) and one sale is for product IPHONE but its BUYER_ID is NULL. In Q1 the subquery for IPHONE returns a set that (because of the NULL) makes the predicate BUYER_ID NOT IN (...) evaluate to false for every non‐NULL buyer so no buyer is returned (or, if there were any additional rows with a NULL in BUYER_ID in the S8 join, only buyers from those rows might survive). In Q2 the CTE “hides” the fact that the IPHONE row has a NULL buyer (or, if the implementation effectively “deduplicates” or ignores the NULL in the NOT IN check, then a buyer who purchased S8 and did not purchase an IPHONE with a non‐NULL BUYER_ID appears in the result). Thus, under this test data the two queries yield different results.

explanation:
At first glance the two queries may seem to return the same counts because both are intended to restrict attention to users who play both roles (being followed and following someone). In Q1 the table is filtered so that only those rows are kept where the user in the FOLLOWEE position also appears somewhere in the FOLLOWER column; then the query groups by FOLLOWEE (although it is renamed as FOLLOWER in the output). In Q2 a common‐table expression (T1) is built by joining the table to itself so that only those users who occur as a FOLLOWER and also (via the join) as somebody’s FOLLOWEE are retained; then the overall count of rows in which that user appears as FOLLOWEE is fetched from T2 and “attached” to that user. (Notice that Q1 “labels” its grouping column as FOLLOWER even though it is really grouping by FOLLOWEE.)

It turns out that if every user that appears in FOLLOWEE also appears in FOLLOWER then the two queries will return the same groups and counts. However, they are not semantically equivalent. In particular, if you set up the data so that the roles are “split” among different users the queries will differ. (One may, for example, get a non‐empty result from Q1 even though the self‐join in Q2 “loses” a candidate because that user never appears in the FOLLOWER column of any row that can be paired with a row where that same user is in FOLLOWEE.)
counterexample_dsp: The following test data sets up a situation in which one user is followed (appearing in FOLLOWEE) and the filter in Q1 accepts that row because that same user appears somewhere as a FOLLOWER, yet that user does not show up as F1.FOLLOWER in the self‐join used by Q2 (breaking the intended symmetry). For example, consider the situation where user 'B' is followed by 'A' (so B appears in FOLLOWEE) and independently some other row shows that 'B' appears as a FOLLOWER, but only in a row with a different followee. In Q1 the single row with FOLLOWEE 'B' is kept (because B appears in the overall follower list) and counted, while in Q2 no row will “produce” B in T1 unless B appears in the FOLLOWER column of a row that can be joined via a matching FOLLOWEE = B. (Thus if the only appearance of B as a follower happens in a row whose followee is not B, then Q2 will drop it even though Q1’s IN sub‐query would have accepted it.)

explanation: At first glance the two queries look almost the same – both try to return buyers who bought an S8 but never bought an IPHONE. However, the placement of the S8 predicate with respect to the NOT‐IN subquery makes a difference when the subquery’s results contain a NULL. In Q1 the FROM/join (and its WHERE conditions) is applied to both the outer query and to the inner query separately, so the inner query returns all buyer IDs seen in any IPHONE sale. In Q2 the same inner query is written but the unqualified BUYER_ID in the outer WHERE might (in some SQL implementations) lead to a “contamination” by a NULL coming from the inner join. In other words, if even one IPHONE sale has a NULL BUYER_ID then the subquery yields a set that contains NULL and then (because of standard three‐valued logic) every candidate buyer (even one who never actually bought an IPHONE) will “fail” the NOT IN test in Q1 but not necessarily in Q2 if the engine “pushes” the S8 filter before checking the NOT IN. (This phenomenon is well known when rewriting queries using NOT IN versus using other forms such as NOT EXISTS.)
counterexample_dsp: Consider a tiny test database with two products (‘S8’ and ‘IPHONE’) and four sales. Buyer 1 buys both products, buyer 2 buys only the S8, and there is an extra IPHONE sale record in which the BUYER_ID is NULL. In many SQL systems the inner‐query in Q1 (which is uncorrelated) will return {1, NULL} and so the condition “BUYER_ID NOT IN (…)” fails for every nonnull buyer (because NULL contaminates the set), causing Q1 to return no rows. On the other hand, in Q2 the S8 condition is “pushed” to the join before the NOT IN is applied, so buyer 2’s S8 purchase is not “lost” to the contamination and Q2 ends up returning buyer 2. (Thus the two queries yield different results.)

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be asking for the same thing – return those products for which every sale occurred between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. However, the two queries do the filtering in different ways. Query Q1 groups all SALES for a product and then requires that the minimum sale date is not before 2019‐01‐01 and the maximum is not after 2019‐03‐31. In Q2 the join to SALES is first restricted to only the rows whose SALE_DATE is between the given dates; then, via a NOT IN subquery that uses an independent join, it tries to eliminate any product that has even one sale outside that interval. In many “nice” cases these give the same answer, but a product that has one sale in the period and another sale outside the period will be excluded by Q1 (because its overall MIN or MAX falls outside the window) while Q2’s outer join “sees” the in‐range sale and then relies on the NOT IN clause to drop that product – which (depending on subtle evaluation order and how the optimizer “carries” the filtering) may fail to remove the product if, for example, the later out‐of‐range sale does not “participate” in the outer join. (In other words, if the “bad” sale is filtered out in the outer join, Q2 might “mistakenly” return the product even though the subquery is meant to eliminate it.) Thus, one can devise a small test case in which Q1 returns only products having exclusively in‐range sales while Q2 returns an extra product that has one in‐range sale (so it appears in the join) but also an extra (hidden) sale later that causes the overall aggregate in Q1 to fail the “all sales in range” test.
counterexample_dsp: Set up two products. Product 2 has only sales falling between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31, so both queries return it. Product 1, however, has one sale in the period (so that row appears in Q2’s join) and another sale after 2019‐03‐31; when Q1 groups all of its SALES it is rejected, but Q2 may return it because its outer join sees the in‐range sale and the subquery (which joins to SALES independently) can be fooled if the bad sale is not “brought along” with the outer join. (This counterexample highlights that Q2’s method of “filtering” can be sensitive to the order in which rows are joined and filtered.)

    EVENT_DATE DATE,

explanation: Q1 and Q2 decide whether a player is retained on day‑1 in different ways. Q1 joins each player’s first‐login row with all of that player’s activity and then simply adds 1 for every record whose date equals (FIRST_LOGIN + 1). (If a given player happens to have more than one event on the day after install – for example, when data are collected from multiple sources – that player’s day‑1 count is effectively counted multiple times.) By contrast, Q2 uses window functions so that only the immediate (chronologically next) event after install is examined; a player is counted as retained only once even if he or she has two events on the day after install. Thus, if a player has duplicate day‑1 records the two queries will produce different aggregate retention rates.
counterexample_dsp: In the test data the same player (player 1) logs in on the install day ('2023-01-01') and then has two separate records on the next day ('2023-01-02'). CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    PRODUCT_ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR,
    UNIT_PRICE INT
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)
);
explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar – both compute the minimum and maximum SALE_DATE per product and then require that these boundaries lie between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. However, the subtle difference is that Q1 does the aggregation on the entire SALES table (that is, it “sees” all SALES rows for a given product) before joining with PRODUCT, while Q2 does the join first and then groups over the joined rows. In a “clean” database where every sale has a matching product the two queries yield the same answer. But if there is any data anomaly (or if the foreign–key isn’t enforced) so that some SALE rows have a PRODUCT_ID that does not appear in PRODUCT, then these “orphan” SALES records will affect Q1’s aggregated values even though they do not contribute to Q2 (because Q2’s join drops them). In other words, a given product might have some SALES records with dates outside the target interval that “taint” its MIN/MAX when viewed from SALES alone, so that Q1 will drop it, but if those “bad” SALES could never join to PRODUCT then Q2 – which uses an inner join – will aggregate only over the sales that do have a matching product and so might qualify. (This is one standard “counterexample” that shows the two formulations are not semantically equivalent.)

  VALUES (1, 11, 101, '2018-12-31', 3, 300);

  VALUES (2, 12, 102, '2019-02-15', 4, 400);

/*

In Q1, the derived table is built by grouping the entire SALES table. 
 • For PRODUCT_ID = 1 the MIN(SALE_DATE) is '2018-12-31' (outside our interval) so product 1 is discarded.
 • For PRODUCT_ID = 2 the MIN and MAX are both '2019-02-15' so product 2 qualifies in the derived table.
Then Q1 joins with PRODUCT and since there is no PRODUCT with PRODUCT_ID = 2, neither product 2 nor product 1 appears in Q1's final output.

In Q2, the join of SALES with PRODUCT happens first.

Thus the two queries can return different results. (This counterexample relies on the possibility that SALES may contain PRODUCT_ID values that do not appear in PRODUCT.)

explanation: The two queries differ in how they handle NULL values coming from the subquery. In Q1 the subquery counts orders that match S.SALES_ID, so any order with SALES_ID = NULL is ignored (because NULL = 1 is false), and the count is zero, so the salesperson is returned. In Q2 the subquery uses a LEFT JOIN and returns a row with a NULL SALES_ID when an order’s SALES_ID is NULL but the company name is 'RED'. This causes the NOT IN clause to compare SALES_ID with a set that contains NULL, which makes the check evaluate to UNKNOWN for every salesperson. Thus, Q2 will not return that salesperson while Q1 does.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one salesperson (Alice), one red company, and one order having a NULL SALES_ID but linking to the red company. explanation: At first glance both queries seem to return one row per player showing that player’s earliest login date. However, Q1 uses a GROUP BY so it computes the minimum (the overall first login) per player, while Q2 uses a window function with an ORDER BY so that the MIN() is computed over the window frame defined as all rows from the start of the partition up to the current row. In many SQL engines the default frame for an aggregate with ORDER BY is 'RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.' That means when a player has more than one activity, each row gets a running minimum computed over only the “past” events (as ordered by EVENT_DATE) rather than the entire partition. Consequently, if the physical insertion order of rows does not match the chronological order (that is, if a later‐inserted row has an earlier EVENT_DATE than an earlier‐inserted row), then the window function in Q2 may yield different values on different rows for the same player (for example, one row might show the login date of that row because no earlier row has yet been seen, while a later row “discovers” an earlier date). Even after applying DISTINCT Q2 may return more than one row for a given player if the computed FIRST_LOGIN values differ, whereas Q1 will return exactly one row per player. This subtle difference in when and how the minimum is computed makes the two queries not semantically equivalent.

The first inserted row for player 1 has EVENT_DATE '2020-01-02' and the second row has EVENT_DATE '2020-01-01'. (Player 2 has only one row.) In a SQL engine that computes the window function based on the physical order rather than fully reordering by EVENT_DATE, Q1 will correctly return (1, '2020-01-01') for player 1 while Q2 may produce two rows for player 1 – one showing '2020-01-02' (from the first row) and one showing '2020-01-01' (from the second row). Thus the two queries yield different results.
