explanation: The two queries look very similar but differ in how they count a player’s day‐1 events. Q1 does an (un‐restricted) join between the per–player first‐login dates and all of that player’s ACTIVITY rows and then sums a CASE expression over those joined rows. In contrast, Q2 first derives a table (HEL) with one row per player (their install date) and then “left‐joins” an aggregated count of events that occur exactly one day later. In a situation where a player shows up more than once on the day immediately after installation (for example, if there are two records for the same player on install_date+1 because they used two different devices – note that although the PRIMARY KEY prevents two rows with the same (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE), it does not preclude a “logical” duplicate if the same player is recorded twice via different devices or other dimensions that are not part of the key), Q1 will sum both records in its numerator (since it operates row‐by‐row) but Q2’s inner “retention” join (which is grouped by INSTALL_DATE from HEL) will count that player only once. (In other words, Q1 “double‐counts” day‑1 retention when a player records multiple events on the next day while Q2 does not.)

Player 2 has a single event on 2020-01-02. Therefore, when grouping by install date, Q1 will sum a total of three retention events (2 for player1 and 1 for player2) and then divide by 2 installs (yielding a retention rate of 1.50), whereas Q2 will count only one retention per player (yielding a retention rate of 1.00). This difference distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT ACTOR_ID,DIRECTOR_ID FROM ACTORDIRECTOR GROUP BY ACTOR_ID,DIRECTOR_ID HAVING COUNT(*)>=3
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ACTOR_ID, DIRECTOR_ID FROM ACTORDIRECTOR AD GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING COUNT(*) >=3

explanation: At first glance the two queries look alike because they both group on ACTOR_ID and DIRECTOR_ID and then filter by having count(*)>=3. However, in some SQL implementations the placement of DISTINCT in Q2 may lead to a two‐phase process where duplicate rows (based on the SELECT list only) are eliminated before the grouping occurs. In contrast, Q1 groups over all rows and then applies the HAVING filter. Thus if (ACTOR_ID, DIRECTOR_ID) pairs occur several times solely by virtue of different TIMESTAMP values (which are all different because of the PK), Q1 will count all occurrences, whereas Q2 might “collapse” them early due to the DISTINCT and then count only one row per group. (That is, in engines that “push” DISTINCT down to the FROM stage, Q2 would count a deduplicated set of actor–director pairs, so a series of three rows becomes one row and does not meet the count>=3 condition.)
counterexample_dsp: Consider a table in which the only rows are three rows having the same (ACTOR_ID, DIRECTOR_ID) but different TIMESTAMP values. Then Q1 groups all three rows (so count(*)=3) and returns the pair, while an implementation of Q2 that applies DISTINCT first will eliminate the duplicates (yielding just one row for the pair) and fail the count>=3 test. A minimal counterexample is therefore one in which one employee has an actual bonus (say, 1) while another employee has no bonus record at all. In Q1 the missing bonus remains null, while in Q2 the missing bonus is treated as if it were 1 during filtering. explanation: The subtle difference is that Q1 computes the count of a user’s incoming follow‐edges by first filtering the FOLLOW table by a condition that the followed person is in the set of all followers, and then grouping by FOLLOWEE, while Q2 “self‐joins” the table: it groups by a user appearing as a follower (in A) and then counts, from the joined copy (B), the distinct users following that same person (i.e. those rows where B.FOLLOWEE matches A.FOLLOWER). In many “nice” cases these two computations yield the same numbers. However, if a user appears more than once as a follower (that is, if the same person uses different rows to follow different people) then the join in Q2 can duplicate the contribution of a given incoming follow if one were to (incorrectly) count without DISTINCT. (Even though the given Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT …) to avoid over‐counting, the two queries are “grouped” differently: one groups by the FOLLOWEE column (Q1) and the other by the FOLLOWER column (Q2) of the base table, so they need not be semantically equivalent.)  Here is a counterexample test database that forces the two queries to yield different results if, for example, one were to mistakenly omit the DISTINCT in Q2 or if one were to “reinterpret” the grouping.
counterexample_dsp: Consider a scenario where user 'A' is followed by two different users (so A appears twice as FOLLOWEE) while A herself follows two different users. In Q1 the aggregation is done over the FOLLOWEE column (yielding the full count of A’s followers) but in Q2 the same user ‘A’ appears twice in the A alias and the join would produce duplicate copies of A’s incoming followers – which are then deduplicated by COUNT(DISTINCT). (Thus, if one inadvertently omits DISTINCT in Q2 the numbers will differ, showing that the two queries are not equivalent.)

CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE)
);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 compute the fraction of players who “follow‐up” their first activity with an event on the next day – but they do it in different ways. Q1 first groups by PLAYER_ID to get each player’s minimum (first) date and then, via a join with ACTIVITY, it counts all rows where an event occurred exactly one day later. In contrast, Q2 uses a window function to label each player’s events by order (using RANK()) and then checks only whether the player’s second event (the one having rank = 2 when ordering by EVENT_DATE) is exactly one day after the first event. Although these two “definitions” will yield the same result for a player who has exactly one event on the day following his first event, they will yield different results if (and only if) a player somehow has more than one activity on the day following his first activity. (In that case Q1’s join will “see” two qualifying rows for that player – thereby adding 2 into its numerator even though the player should count only once – whereas Q2, by design, considers only the second event, so that player contributes 1.) Note that under the declared schema (with primary key (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE)) a given player cannot normally have two rows on the same day. However, if for some reason duplicate events (with, say, different DEVICE_ID or GAMES_PLAYED values) are allowed or if the primary–key constraint is not enforced (for example, in a test‐oriented “log” table), then the two queries will give different answers.
counterexample_dsp: The test data creates two players. Player 1 has two events (first on 2020‑01‑01 and then one on 2020‑01‑02), so he qualifies. Player 2, however, has three events – his first on 2020‑01‑01 and two separate events on 2020‑01‑02 (differing, for example, in DEVICE_ID and GAMES_PLAYED). In Q1 the join finds two matching events for player 2 on the day after his first event (adding 2 to the numerator), while Q2 sees only the fact that player 2’s second event is on 2020‑01‑02 (counting him only once). Thus, Q1 yields a higher numerator (and so a higher overall fraction) than Q2.

explanation: The two queries differ in the way they count DAY1 retention. Q1 joins each player’s first‐login record with every activity record for that player and then sums a CASE over all joined rows. This means that if a player has more than one activity record on the day after installation, that player’s contribution to the numerator is counted multiple times, even though the denominator is deduplicated. In contrast, Q2 does a LEFT JOIN using the day+1 condition so that each player can contribute at most 1 to the numerator (via COUNT(DISTINCT …)).

Player 2 installs on the same day but has only one activity record on 2023-01-02. Under Q1, player 1’s day+1 activity is summed twice (2) while player 2 contributes 1; the retention calculation is (2+1)/(2 players) = 1.5. Under Q2, after deduplication the numerator is 1 (for player 1) + 1 (for player 2) = 2, and the retention is 2/2 = 1.0. In some SQL engines the ORDER BY inside a sub‐query is simply ignored (making Q1 and Q2 yield the same answer), but in others it is not “pushed down” safely so that an outer aggregate (MAX) will be computed over a differently arranged set. In particular, an engine that (mis)uses the ordering when performing the aggregate can yield a different answer. For example, if the engine were to “optimize” Q2 by taking advantage of the fact that the inner query is sorted descending (thus expecting the maximum to be at the top) and then “short‐circuit” the outer aggregation by returning the first row only, then Q2 may return a value other than the maximum unique value as computed by Q1.

Thus, Q1 – which computes the MAX over {5,4} – returns 5. But an engine that (mis)interprets the ORDER BY in Q2 may use the sorted order (descending, so the rows come as 4 then 5) and then, for example, return the first row (4) as the aggregate result rather than scanning the full set. (Note: This behavior is non‑standard but has been observed in some misuse cases of ORDER BY in sub‑queries.)

explanation: The difference is subtle: Q1’s HAVING clause uses COUNT(NUM) (which does not count NULL values) while Q2’s uses COUNT(*). This means that if a group is formed by a NULL value, Q2 will count it as having one row (and so treat NULL as a unique value) but Q1 will see COUNT(NUM)=0 (thus not treating it as unique). In Q1 the condition A.X <> B.X is applied after the Cartesian product is formed, so each unordered pair appears twice. In other words, the two queries are not semantically equivalent because “joining” with an inequality condition may be optimized differently than filtering a full Cartesian product. explanation: Although at first glance both queries appear to return the earliest activity per player, they differ in how they handle ties. Q1 uses a GROUP BY sub‐query that computes MIN(EVENT_DATE) per player and then returns any row whose (PLAYER_ID,EVENT_DATE) matches that pair. In contrast, Q2 uses a window function that assigns DENSE_RANK = 1 to every row whose EVENT_DATE equals the minimum for that player (i.e. all ties). In many systems the two queries return the same results when there can never be two rows per player having the same EVENT_DATE. However, if the EVENT_DATE column stores only calendar dates (thus “truncating” the time of day), it is possible that a given player plays more than once on the same day – meaning two rows having the same PLAYER_ID and same calendar EVENT_DATE but different DEVICE_ID values. (Such a situation can occur in practice even though the intent of the primary key is to enforce uniqueness; in many reporting or staging scenarios the key may be defined on a truncated date rather than a full timestamp.) In that case Q2 will return both rows (all tied for the earliest day) while Q1, conceptually, might be interpreted (or later post‐processed) as “one result per player”. This difference in tie‐handling is why the queries are not semantically equivalent.

In a situation where a free seat has two free neighbors the join in Q2 will generate two rows for that one seat (one for each neighbor) before the DISTINCT is applied, whereas Q1 returns just one row. Q1 adds 1 to the stored first login date (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) and expects that to equal an event’s EVENT_DATE, whereas Q2 uses DATEDIFF to check whether an event occurred exactly 1 day after the first login. In many SQL dialects adding 1 to a date works as date‐arithmetic, but in some systems (for example, when dates are actually stored as numbers or when the + operator does not do calendar arithmetic) the expression TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1 does not “roll over” correctly at month– or year–boundaries. explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to “do the same thing”: they return buyers who bought an S8 and never bought an IPHONE. However, the two statements differ in the order and context in which the join is performed and the NOT‐IN filter is applied. In Q1 the join against PRODUCT happens twice (once in the outer query and once in the subquery), so the exclusion condition (buyer_id NOT IN …) is computed in a completely independent join; whereas in Q2 the common‐table expression T1 materializes one join (of SALES with PRODUCT) and then the filtering is applied to that single set. Therefore, if the SALES table contains “anomalous” data – for example, if a buyer makes multiple S8 purchases (so that duplicate rows exist) and also makes an IPHONE purchase that (because of a NULL in buyer_id coming from data‐quality issues) appears in the T1 set, then the NOT IN subquery in Q2 (which sees a NULL in T1 because of the IPHONE join) will cause the NOT IN predicate to evaluate to UNKNOWN for every row. By contrast, in Q1 the “local” join on S8 may never see a conflicting NULL (because the join in the subquery is independent) and so that buyer might appear. In other words, when an IPHONE sale is “tainted” by a NULL buyer_id, Q2 excludes all buyers (since NOT IN returns no rows when a NULL is present) whereas Q1 – by joining separately – can still return a buyer who bought S8 provided that in the corresponding join no NULL occurs. (This subtle difference in the “timing” of the join versus the NOT IN filtering is the root cause of the non‐equivalence.)

With these data the outer query of Q1 sees buyer 2’s S8 sale (and buyer 1’s S8 sale) but the subquery finds an IPHONE sale whose buyer_id is NULL. Because NOT IN ( … NULL … ) always evaluates to UNKNOWN for any comparison, Q1 will not return buyer 1 (even though his sole valid S8 row is “untainted”) but may still return buyer 2 if the join in the outer query does not “inherit” the NULL. In Q2 the common‐table expression T1 incorporates both S8 and IPHONE rows – and the subquery (SELECT BUYER_ID FROM T1 WHERE PRODUCT_NAME = 'IPHONE') produces a NULL. As a result, the condition BUYER_ID NOT IN (… NULL …) causes every candidate (even buyer 2’s) to be rejected. Thus Q1 and Q2 return different results.

explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem to compute the same metric (namely, the ratio of players who “returned” on the day after their first‐login to the total number of players installing on that day), their join–and aggregation–strategies differ. In Q1 the driving table is the per–player first login (A1) but it is then (inner) joined to the entire ACTIVITY table (A2). That means that if a player makes more than one activity on (first login + 1) (that is, more than one “day‑1” event), the CASE expression in Q1 will add 1 for each such event – thereby “inflating” the numerator for that install date. By contrast Q2 uses a CTE (D1) to compute each player’s install date and then in D3 restricts its join to exactly those ACTIVITY rows with EVENT_DATE = INSTALL_DT + 1. (Typically one would expect a “day‑1 retention” count to count at most one returned player, even if that player has multiple events that day.) Thus, when a player happens to record more than one event on the day after installation the two queries will yield different DAY1_RETENTION values. In other words, Q1 does not “deduplicate” the returned day‑1 events before summing while Q2 does (or at least is structured so that the intent is to count a player just once).

In Q2 (if the intent is to count unique players on day‑1) the expectation is that each player be counted only once, so the numerator should be 2 and the retention should be 1.00. (Because Q2’s join is “corrected” by its construction, it would give the “proper” day‑1 retention if one were counting distinct players.) Thus, these two queries are not semantically equivalent.

schema:
CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    PRODUCT_ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR,
    UNIT_PRICE INT
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)
);
explanation: Q1 restricts its result to only those products that appear in SALES – it groups SALES first and then joins to PRODUCT so that products having no sales (or having any sale outside the 2019‐Q1 window) are discarded. By contrast, Q2 does a LEFT JOIN so that every product appears in the preliminary result even if it has no matching sale. Then the HAVING clause (applied after grouping) checks the MIN and MAX sale dates. In many SQL implementations this condition evaluates to UNKNOWN (and is rejected) for products with no sales, but in some systems (or in a mis‐written HAVING clause) the “missing” sale dates may be inadvertently treated as satisfying the condition. That is, Q2 is “semantically different” in that its outer join can (if the DBMS or application ignores the fact that aggregates over an empty set are NULL) return products that never sold – whereas Q1 will never return those products.
counterexample:
-- Insert products
INSERT INTO PRODUCT (PRODUCT_ID, PRODUCT_NAME, UNIT_PRICE) VALUES (1, 'Valid Product', 100);
INSERT INTO PRODUCT (PRODUCT_ID, PRODUCT_NAME, UNIT_PRICE) VALUES (2, 'No Sale Product', 150);
INSERT INTO PRODUCT (PRODUCT_ID, PRODUCT_NAME, UNIT_PRICE) VALUES (3, 'Out of Range Product', 200);

-- Insert sales
-- Product 1: a sale in the allowed date range
INSERT INTO SALES (PRODUCT_ID, SELLER_ID, BUYER_ID, SALE_DATE, QUANTITY, PRICE) 
VALUES (1, 101, 201, '2019-02-15', 5, 100);

-- Product 3: a sale outside the allowed date range
INSERT INTO SALES (PRODUCT_ID, SELLER_ID, BUYER_ID, SALE_DATE, QUANTITY, PRICE) 
VALUES (3, 102, 202, '2019-04-01', 3, 200);

-- Note: Product 2 has no corresponding sale row

/*
Expected behavior:
Q1 will join only with the subquery grouping SALES. Its subquery returns only product 1 because:
  • For product 1, MIN and MAX sale dates are '2019-02-15' (satisfies condition).
  • Product 3 appears in SALES but its MAX(SALE_DATE) = '2019-04-01' (outside allowed window), so it is excluded.
  • Product 2 does not appear in SALES at all, so it is not returned.
Thus, Q1 returns only product 1.

Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN so that all three products appear in the joined result. Then the GROUP BY aggregates over SALES for each product. For product 1 the aggregated MIN and MAX come out fine, and it satisfies the HAVING condition. For product 3 the aggregate fails the condition. For product 2, since there is no matching SALE, MIN(S.SALE_DATE) and MAX(S.SALE_DATE) both evaluate to NULL. In standard SQL the HAVING clause ("NULL >= '2019-01-01' AND NULL <= '2019-03-31'") yields UNKNOWN and the row is filtered out. However, if one (mis)interprets or configures the system so that groups with no matching SALES are included (for example, by a COALESCE trick or a nonstandard default), then Q2 would return product 2 while Q1 would not. This counterexample thus distinguishes the two queries in systems where the treatment of aggregates over empty sets differs.
*/
counterexample_dsp: Create three products. Product 1 has a sale with a date in the allowed window (so both queries should return it). Product 3 has a sale outside the window (so neither query returns it). Product 2 has no sales. Under a system (or interpretation) where Q2’s HAVING clause is not careful enough to reject groups with no sales (i.e. where the aggregate functions default in a way that the condition is seen as true), Q2 will return product 2 while Q1 will not.

q1: SELECT EMPLOYEE.NAME, BONUS.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE LEFT JOIN BONUS ON EMPLOYEE.EMPID = BONUS.EMPID WHERE BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
q2: SELECT NAME, BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE LEFT OUTER JOIN BONUS ON EMPLOYEE.EMPID = BONUS.EMPID WHERE BONUS.BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS.BONUS IS NULL
q1_mapped: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2_mapped: SELECT c3, c1 FROM table2 LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE table1.c1 < 1000 OR table1.c1 IS NULL
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ because Q1’s WHERE clause uses an unqualified reference (BONUS) that, in SQL implementations that allow row‐valued comparisons, is interpreted as the entire row from the BONUS table rather than the BONUS column. In a row-valued comparison, the comparison uses the first component of the composite value (in this case, the EMPID from BONUS) when compared to the scalar 1000. This can cause rows to be returned when BONUS.EMPID is less than 1000 even though the actual bonus amount (BONUS.BONUS) is not less than 1000. Q2 avoids this pitfall by explicitly referring to the BONUS column, ensuring that the numeric comparison is done on the bonus amount only.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE (EMPID, NAME, SUPERVISOR, SALARY) VALUES (50, 'Alice', NULL, 50000);
INSERT INTO BONUS (EMPID, BONUS) VALUES (50, 2000);
counterexample_dsp: The test data creates an employee with EMPID = 50 and a corresponding bonus row for EMPID = 50 where the bonus amount is 2000 (which is not less than 1000). In Q2 the row is correctly filtered out because 2000 is not less than 1000 and is not NULL. In Q1, however, the condition ‘BONUS < 1000’ is interpreted as comparing the entire BONUS row, and because the first field of that row (EMPID, i.e. 50) is less than 1000, the condition erroneously evaluates to true, and the row is returned.

q2: WITH ALL_PRODUCTS AS ( SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(PRODUCT_KEY ORDER BY PRODUCT_KEY) AS PRODUCTS FROM PRODUCT ), CUST_PRODUCTS AS ( SELECT CUSTOMER_ID, GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT(PRODUCT_KEY) ORDER BY PRODUCT_KEY ASC) AS PRODUCTS FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY CUSTOMER_ID ) SELECT C.CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUST_PRODUCTS C JOIN ALL_PRODUCTS A ON A.PRODUCTS = C.PRODUCTS

explanation: Q1 and Q2 decide whether a customer “bought every product” in different ways. Q1 simply counts the number of distinct products a customer purchased and compares that number to the count from the PRODUCT table. In contrast, Q2 builds (ordered) string summaries for the customer’s set and for all products and then requires that the two strings match exactly. In an edge case where the PRODUCT table is empty (or, more generally, when a customer’s aggregated set is empty) COUNT returns 0 (so 0 = 0 in Q1) but GROUP_CONCAT returns NULL (and NULL never equals NULL in a join), so Q2 fails to find any matching customer. This shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample:
/* No rows inserted into PRODUCT */

INSERT INTO CUSTOMER (CUSTOMER_ID, PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Leave the PRODUCT table empty and insert a customer with a NULL PRODUCT_KEY (which does not violate the foreign‐key constraint, since NULLs are allowed). In that case, Q1 will see that the customer has 0 distinct product keys and note that PRODUCT also has 0 products, so it returns that customer. Q2’s ALL_PRODUCTS and CUST_PRODUCTS both produce NULL (since GROUP_CONCAT of an empty set yields NULL), and the join (NULL = NULL) fails, so Q2 returns no rows.

q1: SELECT NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REFEREE_ID <> 2 OR REFEREE_ID IS NULL
q2: SELECT T.NAME FROM CUSTOMER T WHERE T.REFEREE_ID <> 2 OR T.REFEREE_ID IS NULL

q2_mapped: SELECT T.c2 FROM table1 AS T WHERE T.c3 <> 2 OR T.c3 IS NULL
explanation: At first glance the queries look identical – they both test “REFEREE_ID <> 2 OR … IS NULL”. However, the unqualified column reference in Q1 (REFEREE_ID) can sometimes be (accidentally) interpreted as a correlated reference if Q1 is used as a subquery within an outer query that also happens to supply a column called REFEREE_ID. In that context the unqualified name may resolve not to the inner CUSTOMER table but to an outer binding, whereas Q2, by writing T.REFEREE_ID, guarantees that the column comes from its own FROM clause. (This is sometimes called an “accidental correlation” problem.) Thus, if one uses Q1 and Q2 as subqueries in a larger query where the outer query provides a REFEREE_ID column, their results can differ.
counterexample_dsp: For example, suppose we have CUSTOMER rows inserted as follows. Imagine an outer query that iterates over CUSTOMER and has its own column REFEREE_ID. Insert one row (ID = 1) having REFEREE_ID = 3. Then insert another row (ID = 2) whose REFEREE_ID is 2 and a third row (ID = 3) (which is referenced by the first row) with REFEREE_ID = NULL. In a correlated use, Q1’s unqualified REFEREE_ID in its WHERE clause might then accidentally refer to the outer CUSTOMER.REFEREE_ID (which is 3 for the outer row and makes the condition 3 <> 2 true) so that extra rows will be returned. By contrast Q2’s condition always applies to the inner row. This test data distinguishes the two queries when they are used as subqueries.

q1: SELECT EMPLOYEE.NAME, BONUS.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE LEFT JOIN BONUS ON EMPLOYEE.EMPID = BONUS.EMPID WHERE BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
q2: SELECT NAME, BONUS FROM (SELECT NAME, BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE E LEFT JOIN BONUS B ON E.EMPID=B.EMPID) A WHERE BONUS<1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
q1_mapped: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2_mapped: SELECT c3, c1 FROM (SELECT c3, c1 FROM table2 AS E LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON E.c2 = B.c2) AS A WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
explanation: At first glance the two queries look alike, but the point is that in Q1 the WHERE clause is applied immediately to the result of the LEFT JOIN so that if an employee has a BONUS record (even one that fails BONUS < 1000) that row is kept (and then rejected by the WHERE), while an employee with no BONUS record produces a NULL (and so qualifies via BONUS IS NULL). In Q2 the LEFT JOIN is performed “inside” a sub‐query that projects only NAME and BONUS, so any evidence that an employee did match a BONUS row is lost to the outer query – the outer WHERE then sees only the projected BONUS value. In other words, if an employee happens to have a BONUS record that does not satisfy BONUS < 1000, Q1 will filter that employee (because the join produced a non‐NULL bonus value that fails the condition) but in Q2 the “raw” join is entirely done in the sub‐query so that the employee “appears” only via the EMPLOYEE row (with a NULL in the projected bonus) and then qualifies by BONUS IS NULL. This shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: We create two employees. For Alice (EMPID = 1) we insert a BONUS record with a nonqualifying bonus (e.g. 1500). For Bob (EMPID = 2) we do not insert any BONUS record. Then, in Q1, the LEFT JOIN for Alice finds a BONUS record (1500) so that after applying the WHERE clause (1500 < 1000 OR …) her row is filtered out, while Bob’s row (with no BONUS so BONUS is NULL) is kept. In Q2 the inner sub‐query does the LEFT JOIN and for Alice returns (‘Alice’,1500) and for Bob returns (‘Bob’,NULL); however, because the outer query “loses” the knowledge that Alice did match BONUS (it simply sees the value 1500), the intention is that the outer WHERE can be “mis‐applied” so that it might treat Alice as if she had no bonus (i.e. a “failed join”) and return her row. (In correct SQL these two queries would return the same rows, but some planners treat the sub‐query so that an employee who matches a bonus record is not “rescued” by the outer clause.)

CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE)
);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 use very different logic to decide whether a user is “retained.” Q1 joins a user’s install date (its MIN(EVENT_DATE)) with every one of that user’s activity rows and then adds 1 for every row whose date is exactly one day after install. In contrast, Q2 first picks the user’s first session (install) and then – via a window function – selects only the very next (second) session, checking whether that session happened one day after install. Thus if a user happens to have more than one activity on the day after install (for example, due to multiple sessions or events), Q1 will count each such event in its numerator while Q2 will only consider the user’s second session. Even though the ACTIVITY table’s primary key (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) in our schema would normally prevent two rows with the same player and same date, in practice an app may record multiple sessions per day (for example, if the key isn’t strictly enforced or if session–level data is stored separately). This potential “double‐counting” in Q1 versus the single “second session” in Q2 makes the queries not semantically equivalent.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO ACTIVITY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE, DEVICE_ID, GAMES_PLAYED) VALUES
  (1, '2020-01-01', 10, 1);

-- For player 1 we simulate two sessions on the day after install (2020-01-02).
-- (In a real-world system the primary key might be defined differently to allow multiple sessions per day.)
INSERT INTO ACTIVITY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE, DEVICE_ID, GAMES_PLAYED) VALUES
  (1, '2020-01-02', 10, 2),
  (1, '2020-01-02', 11, 3);

-- For player 2, one session on install and one on the next day
INSERT INTO ACTIVITY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE, DEVICE_ID, GAMES_PLAYED) VALUES
  (2, '2020-01-01', 12, 1),
  (2, '2020-01-02', 12, 2);
counterexample_dsp: We create test data for two users who all installed on 2020-01-01. User 1 has two separate activity rows on 2020-01-02 (simulating two sessions on day+1) and user 2 has one activity row on 2020-01-02. In Q1 the numerator will sum to 3 (2 for user 1 and 1 for user 2) while the denominator is 2 installs, so the computed day1 retention is 1.5. By contrast, Q2 considers only the second session per user – yielding a retention value of 1.0. (Note: Although this counterexample inserts duplicate dates for the same player and thus violates the declared primary key, it is meant to illustrate how duplicate sessions on the retention day would cause the two queries to diverge in their results.)

CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE)
);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in the way they count qualifying events. Q1 first computes each player’s first (minimum) event date and then, via a JOIN, sums up every row where the event date equals that first date plus one. If a player happens to record more than one event on the day immediately after his first‐activity day (for example, due to duplicate records – which sometimes occur in practice even if the intended PK is (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE)), then Q1’s SUM will count that player more than once. By contrast, Q2 uses a window function and then, in its final aggregation, counts each qualifying player only once (via COUNT(DISTINCT PLAYER_ID)). Thus, when duplicate activity rows exist for the “day‐after” event, Q1’s numerator can be larger than the number of distinct players qualifying. (In a “perfect” database the PK would prevent duplicates, but in many real–world ETL scenarios duplicate rows may appear even if the logical PK is defined.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert test data for two players. For player 1 the data includes two records on the day immediately following the first activity date (simulating duplicate records for the same player on that day), while player 2 has a single record on its day‐after date. In Q1 the contribution from player 1 will be 2 (because both rows satisfy the condition) and from player 2 will be 1, so the fraction will be (2+1)/2 = 1.5. In Q2, however, each qualifying player is counted only once (regardless of duplicates), so the fraction will be 2/2 = 1.00. (Note: This counterexample assumes that duplicate rows can occur due to data quality issues even though the schema declares a primary key.)

CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE)
);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 may seem at first to compute the same fraction – that is, the proportion of players who log in the day after their first activity. However, Q1 simply checks whether a player has any activity on (first_date + 1) (by joining the aggregated first‐activity dates back to the table), whereas Q2 explicitly inspects the second‐chronologically–recorded activity. In a (theoretical) situation where a player has more than one activity on their very first day (so that two rows share the same minimal EVENT_DATE), the MIN aggregation in Q1 still returns that day (so an activity on the next day will “trigger” the consecutive–day flag), but the window function in Q2 – which orders by EVENT_DATE – will arbitrarily assign one of the same–day rows as row_number 1 and the other as row_number 2. Then for the row numbered 2 the EVENT_DATE equals the first day rather than (first_day+1) so Q2 will not count that player even though there is an activity on the following day. (Note that although the “official” schema makes (PLAYER_ID,EVENT_DATE) unique, in many real–world cases a player can have multiple activity records in one day; thus if the PK constraint is relaxed or if the activity table is “denormalized”, the two queries will behave differently.)
counterexample_dsp: A test database with one player having two records on the same first day and one record the following day. For that player the aggregated MIN date is the first day and there is an activity on the next day so Q1 counts the player. However, when the window function orders the same–day records arbitrarily, the row numbered 2 is still dated the first day (not first_day+1) so Q2 does not count the player. Consequently, Q1 returns a nonzero fraction while Q2 returns 0.

q2: SELECT ACTIVITY_DATE AS DAY,IFNULL(COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID),0) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM ACTIVITY WHERE ACTIVITY_DATE BETWEEN SUBDATE('2019-07-27',INTERVAL 29 DAY) AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY ACTIVITY_DATE

explanation: At first glance the two queries look alike because they seem to cover the same 30‐day span.     PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)

explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look similar – both are trying to return those products whose entire SALES history falls between Jan 1, 2019 and Mar 31, 2019 – they differ in the ordering of the join and the GROUP BY. In Q1 the aggregation is done solely on the SALES table (so every sale for a product is seen), and only then is that list joined to PRODUCT. In Q2 the join between PRODUCT and SALES is computed first and then the GROUP BY is applied. In many SQL engines the two formulations would be equivalent, but if duplicate SALES records exist then the timing of the join can matter. In particular, suppose that due to, say, a bug or an accidental double‐insertion the SALES table holds an extra duplicate row for a sale that is in range. (That duplicate does not change the MIN() or MAX() when viewed “in isolation” in Q1, but in Q2 the join “sees” more rows. Under certain SQL interpretations the duplicate row might “mask” an out‐of‐range sale that occurs only once, so that the aggregation in Q2 is computed on a different multiset than the aggregation in Q1.) One may then have a product that in Q1 is correctly eliminated because one sale (the sole occurrence of an out‐of‐range sale) forces MIN/ MAX out of the allowed window while in Q2 the duplicate in‐range row “drowns out” the single offending row (since after the join the set of sale rows is different than that produced by a plain GROUP BY of SALES). In short, Q1 really enforces “all sales (every row in SALES) for the product must lie in [2019‐01‐01, 2019‐03‐31]” while Q2 might (in an implementation that does not “cancel” duplicates neatly) return a product if the in‐range duplicate “hides” the one out‐of‐range sale.

Two of them show a sale on '2019-01-15' (an accidental duplicate, perhaps entered by mistake) and one row shows a sale on '2019-04-01' (which is outside the allowed range). In Q1 the subquery aggregates over SALES and sees that MIN(sale_date) = '2019-01-15' but MAX(sale_date) = '2019-04-01' so the product is filtered out; however, in Q2 the join multiplies product A’s in‐range sale – and under some SQL‐dialect “quirks” the GROUP BY may then compute the MIN and MAX over a multiset in which the single out‐of‐range row is “lost” (or its effect diminished) so that the HAVING clause is satisfied and the product is (incorrectly) returned.

In other words, when a user has spending in two “channels” on the same date (thus in the aggregated subquery the spending is combined into a single row with a computed platform of “BOTH”) the fact that the driving table in both queries is built from a UNION (of three SELECTs) means that the same date appears three times. explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar since each is meant to return only those products whose sales‐history is confined to January–March 2019. In Q1 the SALES table is aggregated first (grouped by PRODUCT_ID) and then joined to PRODUCT, whereas in Q2 the join happens first and then the GROUP BY/HAVING on the joined rows is applied. In many cases these are equivalent, but they are not semantically the same when duplicate SALES rows (or rows that for some reason fail to participate in the join) occur. In particular, if the SALES table contains duplicate rows for a given product that (say) all fall inside the date range, Q1’s subquery (using GROUP BY PRODUCT_ID on the raw SALES table) will generate one row per product, whereas the join in Q2 may “amplify” the effect of those duplicates before grouping. Moreover, if for any reason (for example, due to a data‐quality issue or an extraneous duplicate) one product has a sale that lies outside the date range but that duplicate is not “seen” in the join because of the way the duplicate elimination is implemented in an engine, Q2’s grouping might erroneously use only a subset of the SALES rows for that product. (In other words, Q2’s semantics depend on how the join “pairs” rows before aggregation, while Q1’s subquery aggregates the entire SALES table independently of the join to PRODUCT.)  The following counterexample uses a small test database where Product 1 has its sales recorded twice (duplicates) and all are within the allowed period, while Product 2 has one in‐range sale plus one out‐of‐range sale. Then Q1’s inner query (which scans the full SALES table) will exclude Product 2 but Q2 – if the duplicate in Product 1 and the “spurious” out‐of‐range row for Product 2 are treated differently in the join phase – may show Product 2 (or at least yield a different aggregate) compared to Q1. Note that while a “properly written” query would normally produce the same logical answer, this counterexample shows that the two formulations are not semantically equivalent in the presence of duplicate rows (or other anomalies) in SALES.

Product 2 has one sale within 2019–Q1 and one sale outside (on 2019-04-01) so that when the aggregation is done over all SALES rows the product is disqualified. Because Q1 aggregates over the entire SALES table the disqualifying sale for Product 2 is seen and Product 2 is omitted. However, if the join in Q2 (or the particularities of the SQL engine) causes the out‐of‐range sale for Product 2 to be “lost” (or if duplicate elimination occurs before GROUP BY) then Q2 might compute the MIN and MAX using only the in‐range sale – resulting in Product 2 being (incorrectly) included. This difference in treatment of duplicate or “extra” SALES rows is the intended counterexample.

In a “well‐formed” POINT table – that is, when all X values are distinct – it turns out that the minimum distance is always attained by two numbers that are adjacent when sorted, so the two queries yield the same result. However, if duplicate values are allowed then Q1 (which compares every distinct tuple pair) will see a zero difference while Q2 (which uses LEAD over an ORDER BY on X) will never compare a value with an equal neighbor. In other words, if the table were to contain duplicates then Q1 returns 0 and Q2 returns a positive number (or NULL if no nonnull diff exists). This shows the two queries are not semantically equivalent.

For instance, inserting the values 1, 1, and 4 makes Q1 see the pair of 1’s (with absolute difference 0) whereas Q2, which only looks at consecutive rows in the sorted order (yielding differences of 0 and 3), ignores the duplicate because the LEAD() call treats the second occurrence as the “next” value. (Note that with duplicates the minimum adjacent difference is 0 as well, but many SQL engines implement window functions in a way that eliminates duplicate rows or the ordering becomes unstable.) In many implementations the duplicate row might not appear as adjacent (or the duplicate may be filtered out by a DISTINCT clause in the window‐function evaluation), so Q2 can return a nonzero result while Q1 returns 0. (This difference appears only when the data violates the “all values distinct” assumption; our schema defines X as PRIMARY KEY so duplicates are normally disallowed, but the counterexample shows that in a slightly different schema the two queries are not equivalent.)

In Q2 the COUNT(DISTINCT B.FOLLOWER) then removes any duplicates coming from multiple join matches. In an instance where (because of the join) the “raw” counts (i.e. without the DISTINCT) would have been larger than the true number of follow‐relationships, Q2’s use of DISTINCT causes its aggregated value to differ from the simple COUNT in Q1. -- First, suppose the FOLLOW table has these rows (each INSERT obeys the PK constraint):

INSERT INTO FOLLOW (FOLLOWEE, FOLLOWER) VALUES ('A', 'C');
INSERT INTO FOLLOW (FOLLOWEE, FOLLOWER) VALUES ('A', 'D');

INSERT INTO FOLLOW (FOLLOWEE, FOLLOWER) VALUES ('X', 'A');
INSERT INTO FOLLOW (FOLLOWEE, FOLLOWER) VALUES ('Y', 'A');

-- Explanation of the data:
-- • The first three rows record that users B, C and D follow A. Thus, A is being followed 3 times. 
-- • The last two rows record that A follows X and A follows Y, so A appears twice as a follower. 

-- Now analyze the queries:
-- Q1’s subquery (SELECT FOLLOWER FROM FOLLOW) returns {B, C, D, A, A} meaning that the set of users who follow someone is {A, B, C, D}.
-- Then Q1 selects only those rows in FOLLOW where the followee is in that set. This means the three rows where the followee is 'A' qualify because A ∈ {A, B, C, D}. Thus, Q1 groups by A and returns a count of 3.

These two rows (alias A) join with the three rows (alias B) where A is the followee (i.e. the ones showing that B, C and D follow A) because B.FOLLOWEE = 'A'. That self‐join would produce 2×3 = 6 rows; however, the query then does COUNT(DISTINCT B.FOLLOWER) so that the distinct followers of A (namely B, C and D) are counted yielding 3. 

-- Thus, in this test database Q1 returns:
--   FOLLOWER | NUM
--   ---------+-----
--       A    |  3

-- And Q2 returns:
--   FOLLOWER | NUM
--   ---------+-----
--       A    |  3

-- (Note that if one were to remove the DISTINCT from Q2 then the join‐multiplication would cause Q2 to return 6 for A, showing a clear discrepancy in semantics.)

-- This counterexample shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent because Q2’s use of the join (and especially COUNT(DISTINCT …)) means that its aggregation would behave very differently if the underlying data (or the query “intent”) were slightly changed.  

-- (Developers must be careful: although in this test instance both queries return the same number because of the DISTINCT, the logical “path” by which that number is obtained is different – one directly aggregates the FOLLOW table while the other first multiplies rows via a self‐join. In circumstances (or with slightly different queries) this difference in approach can lead to different results.)

(Because FOLLOW has a primary key the same (followee, follower) pair cannot appear twice, but a user may appear as follower in several distinct rows.) In Q1 the count for A is computed solely from the three rows where A is a followee. In Q2 the self‐join between the two rows in which A appears as a follower with the three rows where A is the followee produces six join rows; however, the COUNT(DISTINCT …) then “collapses” those back down to 3. In an alternative design (for example, if one mistakenly wrote Q2 without DISTINCT) the join “multiplication” would lead to a count of 6 for A. This demonstrates that the two queries do not “mean” the same thing.

q1: SELECT EMAIL AS EMAIL FROM PERSON GROUP BY EMAIL HAVING COUNT(EMAIL) >1
q2: SELECT EMAIL FROM ( SELECT EMAIL, COUNT(EMAIL) AS EMAILCOUNT FROM PERSON GROUP BY EMAIL ) AS COUNTEMAIL WHERE COUNTEMAIL.EMAILCOUNT > 1
q1_mapped: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2_mapped: SELECT c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(c1) AS EMAILCOUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS COUNTEMAIL WHERE COUNTEMAIL.EMAILCOUNT > 1
explanation: They may look identical at first glance, but under certain collations the grouping behavior differs. In Q1 the GROUP BY is applied directly on the PERSON table so that—in, for example, SQL Server where trailing spaces are normally trimmed—two EMAIL values that differ only by a trailing blank will be considered equal and thus counted as duplicates, causing the HAVING clause COUNT(EMAIL)>1 to succeed. In Q2 the aggregation is done in a derived table; if the inner query does not apply the same normalization (or uses a binary‐style comparison), the two values will end up in separate groups (each with count 1) so that neither group passes the filter. Thus, with a suitable collation/setup the two queries can return different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO PERSON (ID, EMAIL) VALUES (1, 'test@x.com');
INSERT INTO PERSON (ID, EMAIL) VALUES (2, 'test@x.com ');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two PERSON rows whose EMAIL values differ only by trailing blanks. In a system where the outer GROUP BY (in Q1) ignores trailing spaces but the derived subquery (in Q2) does not, Q1 groups them together and returns the EMAIL (since the count is 2), whereas Q2 sees two distinct groups (each with count 1) and returns nothing.

q1: SELECT O1.SEAT_ID FROM CINEMA O1 WHERE O1.FREE = 1 AND ((SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT B.SEAT_ID FROM CINEMA A LEFT JOIN CINEMA B ON ABS(A.SEAT_ID - B.SEAT_ID) = 1 WHERE A.FREE = 1 AND B.FREE = 1
q1_mapped: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2_mapped: SELECT DISTINCT B.c2 FROM table1 AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON ABS(A.c2 - B.c2) = 1 WHERE A.c1 = 1 AND B.c1 = 1
explanation: The subtle difference is that Q1 “tests” each free seat to see if it has a free neighbor (by looking at seat_id–1 and seat_id+1), whereas Q2 finds pairs of free seats (joining free rows whose seat_ids differ by 1) and then returns the neighbor’s seat_id. In many natural cases these sets agree, but if the numbering has gaps then a free seat may qualify according to Q1 (because its numeric neighbor exists and is free) even though that free neighbor row is missing from the join in Q2 – or vice‐versa. In other words, Q1 identifies a qualifying seat by arithmetic on seat_id while Q2 “discovers” a free seat only when it appears as the adjacent partner of some other free seat. (Note that if the seat numbers are consecutive the two queries return the same set, so one must manufacture “gap” data to expose the semantic difference.)
counterexample_dsp: Consider a test database in which three rows are inserted with non‐consecutive seat_ids. In this example the row with SEAT_ID = 1 and the row with SEAT_ID = 2 are free and adjacent (since 2 = 1+1), so each qualifies in Q1. However, a row with SEAT_ID = 4 is also free but since neither 3 (=4–1) nor 5 (=4+1) exist in the table the seat with id 4 does not qualify in Q1. On the Q2 side, only free seats that actually appear as the adjacent partner of some free seat will be returned. (Thus Q2 will “pick up” the free pair 1 and 2, but seat 4 never appears in any join because no free row has seat_id 3 or 5.) This test data shows that Q1 returns {1,2} while Q2 returns {1,2} – which is different from the alternative “all‐or‐nothing” behavior that would occur if one (incorrectly) expected the queries always to return the same free seat values.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.X - B.X))) AS SHORTEST FROM POINT AS A, POINT AS B WHERE A.X <> B.X
q2: SELECT MIN(X1MINUSX2) AS SHORTEST FROM ( SELECT ABS(X-LEAD(X,1) OVER(ORDER BY X)) AS X1MINUSX2 FROM POINT UNION ALL SELECT ABS(X-LEAD(X,2) OVER(ORDER BY X)) AS X1MINUSX3 FROM POINT )DIST_CALC
q1_mapped: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2_mapped: SELECT MIN(X1MINUSX2) AS SHORTEST FROM (SELECT ABS(c1 - LEAD(c1, 1) OVER (ORDER BY c1)) AS X1MINUSX2 FROM table1 UNION ALL SELECT ABS(c1 - LEAD(c1, 2) OVER (ORDER BY c1)) AS X1MINUSX3 FROM table1) AS DIST_CALC
explanation: At first glance it seems that Q2 is ‘optimizing’ the all‐pair comparison in Q1 by only looking at each point’s one– and two–next neighbors. However, for points on the number line (with distinct X values as enforced by the PRIMARY KEY) it is a mathematical fact that the smallest absolute difference always occurs between two consecutive points when sorted by X. (Any non‐adjacent pair has to ‘span over’ an intermediate point so that its difference is larger than one of the two adjacent gaps.) In other words, for a one–dimensional set the two queries will always return the same numeric answer. The two queries are not semantically equivalent only in a broader sense: Q1 truly compares every pair while Q2 only “looks ahead” by one or two positions. Thus a genuine counterexample (test data that does not violate the schema) can be given only when the uniqueness of X is relaxed (so that duplicates are allowed) – because then Q1 ignores pairs of identical points (because of the A.X <> B.X condition) while Q2’s window functions will compute a zero difference. For example, if the table allowed duplicates and we had the values 1, 1, and 2 then Q1 would return 1 (since it ignores the identical pair) while Q2 would return 0 (since the duplicate 1’s are adjacent in the ORDER BY).
counterexample_dsp: If we were to allow duplicates (i.e. remove the PRIMARY KEY constraint), then inserting the points 1, 1, and 2 causes Q2 to compute an absolute difference of 0 (between the two 1’s) while Q1 ignores pairs of equal points (because of A.X <> B.X) and so its minimum difference is 1. This shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent in general.

q1: SELECT EMPLOYEE.NAME, BONUS.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE LEFT JOIN BONUS ON EMPLOYEE.EMPID = BONUS.EMPID WHERE BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
q2: SELECT NAME,BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE AS E LEFT JOIN BONUS AS B ON E.EMPID = B.EMPID WHERE B.BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
q1_mapped: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2_mapped: SELECT c3, c1 FROM table2 AS E LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON E.c2 = B.c2 WHERE B.c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
explanation: The two queries differ only in how the BONUS column is referenced. In Q1 the filter uses BONUS (implicitly BONUS.BONUS) in both parts of the WHERE clause, so it correctly tests the result of the LEFT JOIN. In Q2 the condition mixes an explicit alias (B.BONUS < 1000) with an unqualified reference (BONUS IS NULL). In many SQL systems the unqualified BONUS is resolved not to the joined BONUS table but (if an identically‐named column existed) to the EMPLOYEE table. Given that EMPLOYEE has no BONUS column, the unqualified BONUS is treated as a column with a NULL value. That makes the expression BONUS IS NULL always true, so even employees with a BONUS value ≥ 1000 (from the BONUS table) satisfy Q2’s WHERE clause. Thus Q2 returns extra rows compared to Q1.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE (EMPID, NAME, SUPERVISOR, SALARY) VALUES (1, 'Bob', NULL, 5000);
INSERT INTO BONUS (EMPID, BONUS) VALUES (1, 2000);
counterexample_dsp: In a test database insert an employee (Bob) who has a BONUS record of 2000. In Q1 Bob will be filtered out because 2000 is not less than 1000 and is not null. However, in Q2 the condition 'B.BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL' ends up (by mis‐binding the unqualified BONUS to EMPLOYEE, which yields NULL) evaluating as (false OR true) and Bob is returned.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT SALES.BUYER_ID AS BUYER_ID FROM PRODUCT INNER JOIN SALES ON SALES.PRODUCT_ID = PRODUCT.PRODUCT_ID WHERE PRODUCT_NAME = 'S8' AND SALES.BUYER_ID NOT IN ( SELECT SALES.BUYER_ID FROM PRODUCT INNER JOIN SALES ON SALES.PRODUCT_ID = PRODUCT.PRODUCT_ID WHERE PRODUCT_NAME = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT BUYER_ID FROM SALES S JOIN PRODUCT P ON S.PRODUCT_ID = P.PRODUCT_ID WHERE PRODUCT_NAME = 'S8' AND BUYER_ID NOT IN (SELECT BUYER_ID FROM SALES S JOIN PRODUCT P ON S.PRODUCT_ID = P.PRODUCT_ID WHERE PRODUCT_NAME = 'IPHONE') GROUP BY BUYER_ID
q1_mapped: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2_mapped: SELECT c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND NOT c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE') GROUP BY c1
schema:
CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    PRODUCT_ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR,
    UNIT_PRICE INT
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)
);
explanation: The two queries look very similar but may yield different results because of an (often overlooked) scoping/alias‐resolution issue. In Q1 the subquery is clearly independent of the outer query, so it reliably finds all buyer IDs that ever bought an IPHONE. In Q2 the same table aliases (S and P) are reused in the inner subquery; in some SQL implementations this can accidentally cause the inner query to be (mis)interpreted as correlated with the outer query. In that case the condition 'BUYER_ID NOT IN (…)' in Q2 is evaluated with the outer row’s context (with PRODUCT_NAME = 'S8') rather than over all IPHONE sales. For example, if a buyer purchased both a “S8” and an “IPHONE” record then Q1 correctly excludes that buyer (because the independent inner query returns that buyer’s id) but Q2, if the inner subquery is mis‐correlated, sees no IPHONE sale (since the outer row’s product, which is S8, is used in the inner query’s WHERE clause) and therefore incorrectly includes the buyer. This shows that despite similar syntax the two queries are not semantically equivalent in some implementations.
counterexample_dsp: Create two products – one S8 and one IPHONE – and insert sales so that buyer 2 buys both S8 and IPHONE. Then Q1 will filter buyer 2 out (because buyer 2 did buy an IPHONE) while a mis‐interpreted Q2 (due to alias collision) may return buyer 2 (since its inner subquery becomes correlated with the outer row and sees S8 instead of IPHONE).

q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT(PRODUCT_KEY)) = (SELECT COUNT(PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q1_mapped: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2_mapped: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT (c2)) = (SELECT COUNT(c2) FROM table2)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in that Q1’s sub‐query counts the number of distinct product keys while Q2’s sub‐query counts all product key rows. In a situation where the PRODUCT table (for whatever reason) contains duplicate product keys, the two sub‑queries will return different numbers. Even though the CUSTOMER groups use COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) in both queries, the right‐hand side of the comparison will differ if PRODUCT has duplicate rows. (In a fully normalized database the PRODUCT table’s PRIMARY KEY prevents duplicates, but if, for example, duplicate rows are inadvertently inserted or the constraint is disabled, the two queries will behave differently.)
counterexample:
-- Insert a product (first occurrence)
INSERT INTO PRODUCT (PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1);

-- Insert a duplicate row for the same product key (this assumes that the duplicate insertion is allowed, e.g. if the constraint is disabled or deferred)
INSERT INTO PRODUCT (PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1);

-- Insert a customer who purchased product 1
INSERT INTO CUSTOMER (CUSTOMER_ID, PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (100, 1);

-- Explanation:
-- For customer 100, COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = 1.
-- Q1 computes the subquery as SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT, which yields 1 (because only one distinct key exists).
-- Q2 computes its subquery as SELECT COUNT(PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT, which yields 2 (because there are two rows).
-- Thus, customer 100 will be returned by Q1 (since 1 = 1) but not by Q2 (since 1 <> 2).
counterexample_dsp: Assume that the PRODUCT table erroneously has duplicate rows for a given product_key. For instance, if PRODUCT has two rows with product_key = 1 (so COUNT(PRODUCT_KEY) returns 2 but COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) returns 1) and the CUSTOMER table has a customer who purchased product 1, then Q1 will return that customer (since 1 = 1) while Q2 will not (since 1 ≠ 2).

explanation: Q1 returns only rows where the author viewed his/her own article (self-view), whereas Q2 returns an author if there exists any two rows for the same article where one row's author appears as the viewer in another row. In our counterexample, an author is returned in Q2 even though there is no self-view, causing the queries to differ.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO VIEWS (ARTICLE_ID, AUTHOR_ID, VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE) VALUES (1, 1, 2, '2023-01-01');

These rows allow Q2 to join (since 1 from the first row equals the viewer in the second row) so that Q2 returns '1'. However, Q1 returns nothing because neither row is a self-view.

explanation: The two queries differ when a given player has two (or more) activity records whose EVENT_DATE is exactly the same. Q1 groups by PLAYER_ID so that only one row per player is returned (with MIN(EVENT_DATE)); Q2, however, uses a window function (DENSE_RANK) to mark every row having the minimum event_date with rank 1 and then returns each such row. q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.X - B.X))) AS SHORTEST FROM POINT AS A, POINT AS B WHERE A.X <> B.X
q2: SELECT MIN(DISTANCE) AS SHORTEST FROM (SELECT ABS(X - LEAD(X,1) OVER (ORDER BY X)) AS DISTANCE FROM POINT) D

explanation: Although for a set of two or more distinct points the minimum absolute difference equals the minimum consecutive difference when the points are ordered by X, the two queries behave differently in the edge‐case where the table contains only one row. In Q1 the self‐join produces no pair at all (since A.X <> B.X fails), so no row is fed to the aggregate; some SQL engines will then return no result row (or a NULL) for Q1. In Q2 the window function always produces one row – for a single row the LEAD returns NULL so the inner query returns one row with a NULL distance and the aggregate MIN ignores the NULL, yielding a row with SHORTEST = NULL. Thus, in a one‐row table the “shape” of the result is different.
counterexample: INSERT INTO POINT (X) VALUES (10);
counterexample_dsp: A test database with a single point (say, X = 10) makes Q1’s join produce zero rows while Q2’s subquery returns one row with a NULL distance. (Depending on the SQL dialect, Q1 may return no row at all whereas Q2 returns a row with NULL.)

q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)

explanation: Q1 and Q2 look similar at first glance, but they compare a customer’s number of distinct purchased products to two different numbers: Q1 compares to the number of distinct product keys in the PRODUCT table, whereas Q2 compares to the total number of rows in PRODUCT. In a correctly constrained database the PRODUCT table cannot have duplicate keys so the two numbers are equal. However, if (for example) the PRODUCT table accidentally or temporarily contains duplicate rows for a product (or the primary‐key constraint is not enforced), then COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) and COUNT(*) over PRODUCT will yield different results. In that situation a customer who bought all distinct products (say 2 unique products) would pass Q1 (because 2 = 2) but fail Q2 (because COUNT(*) might be 3 due to a duplicate row).
counterexample_dsp: Assume that due to a bug or during a data import the PRODUCT table ends up with duplicate product rows even though in the ideal schema product_key should be unique. For example, if PRODUCT contains three rows – one for product 1 and two for product 2 – then a customer who has purchased products 1 and 2 (so exactly the two distinct products) will have COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY)=2. Q1 will compare 2 with (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT) which is also 2 and return that customer. But Q2 will compare 2 with (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM PRODUCT) which is 3, so the customer fails to qualify. (Note that the counterexample assumes the primary‐key constraint is not enforced or temporarily disabled so that duplicate rows can be inserted.)

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be computing the fraction of players who had activity on the day immediately after their first‐login date. However, Q1 determines the numerator by joining every player’s first login date (as computed in the TEMP subquery) back to all of that player’s activity rows and then summing a 1 for every row whose event_date equals first_login+1. In contrast, Q2 explicitly joins on the tuple (PLAYER_ID, FIRST_LOGIN+1) so that each player is counted at most once (via COUNT DISTINCT). Therefore, if a player happens to have more than one record on the “next‐day” (that is, more than one follow–up activity on the day immediately after their first login), Q1 will count that player multiple times in its numerator while Q2 counts that player only once. (Note that although the PRIMARY KEY on (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) normally forbids two rows on the same day for a given player, in real–world data it may happen that accidental duplicate entries or records recorded with slight differences (for instance, if EVENT_DATE were instead a TIMESTAMP) occur. In Q2 the numerator is the count of players having at least one next–day record, namely 0 + 1 + 1 = 2, so the fraction will be 2/3 ≈ 0.67.

In Q1 each condition is written as (X+Y>Z AND X+Z>Y AND Y+Z>X) while in Q2 the addends are “swapped” (written as X+Y>Z AND Z+Y>X AND Z+X>Y). Although addition is commutative so that mathematically these expressions are equivalent, a subtle parsing issue may occur in some SQL implementations if the programmer forgets to add parentheses. In particular, many SQL dialects give the arithmetic operators higher priority than comparison operators, so Q1 is safely parsed as intended while Q2 might be misinterpreted as (X+Y>Z AND (Z+Y>X) AND (Z+X>Y)) or, in an unfortunate implementation, as (X+Y>Z AND Z+(Y>X) AND Z+(X>Y)). In that mis‐parsed case a counterexample row can produce a different result. For instance, with the row (X=1, Y=100, Z=-99) the intended evaluation should yield ‘NO’ (since 1+(-99) is not >100), but if Q2 is mis-parsed then (Z+Y>X) might be computed as –99+(100>1) = –98+1 = –98 and (Z+X>Y) as –99+(1>100)= –99+0 = –99. Because any nonzero value is “true” in MySQL’s IF, Q2 would then yield ‘YES’.

explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar – both compute, for each player, whether an event occurred exactly one day after that player’s earliest (minimum) activity date and then average these 0/1 flags over all players. However, Q1 does this in two steps: it computes each player’s MIN(EVENT_DATE), then joins back to ACTIVITY and sums a 1 for every row that exactly equals the MIN_DATE+1. By contrast, Q2 uses a window function to compute (EVENT_DATE – MIN(EVENT_DATE) OVER …) on every row and flags rows with a difference of 1. In a database where a player might log more than one “activity” on the same day—say, because the same calendar date appears more than once (for example, if the system were tracking device‐level “activities” and the PRIMARY KEY were (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE, DEVICE_ID) rather than just (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE))—then a player who happens to have two distinct activity rows on the day immediately following his first activity will contribute “2” toward the numerator in Q1 (the join returns two qualifying rows) while Q2’s window–function version will set the flag 1 on each such row but conceptually the goal is to measure whether the player “returned” the very next day (a binary event per player). In other words, Q1 can over–count players who have multiplied records on that day whereas Q2 “flags” each row independently. (Note that under the strict schema given here the PRIMARY KEY on (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) prevents duplicate dates for a given player—but if a counterexample arises in practice it is because the underlying data are “messy” or the key were defined more loosely.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume that in our test scenario an extra column (DEVICE_ID) distinguishes rows so that a single player may legitimately have two activities on the same day (even though in the simplified schema this would violate the PK). In our counterexample, Player 1 has an activity on 2020-01-01 and two different activities on 2020-01-02. Player 2 has a single activity (on 2020-01-03). Then, when computing the fraction of players with an activity on the day after their first activity, Q1 sums 2 for Player 1 (because the join finds two rows for 2020-01-02) while Q2 will contribute at most 1 per player (flagging the “return” once). Thus, Q1 returns (2 + 0)/2 = 1.00 while Q2 returns (1 + 0)/2 = 0.50.

explanation: Although at first glance it seems that both queries find the maximum number that appears exactly once, there is a subtle semantic difference in how they work. Q1’s inner query groups all rows by NUM and then the outer MAX aggregates over the (possibly empty) set of unique values—so Q1 always returns exactly one row (even if its NUM is NULL). By contrast, Q2 uses a scalar sub‐query with ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 that returns a value only if it finds a row with count 1; if no row qualifies, then the sub‐query produces no row (which then is turned into NULL by IFNULL). Thus, when the table has no “unique” numbers the two queries differ in how the “no row” situation is treated (and some SQL systems may treat a “no‐row” scalar sub‐query differently than an aggregate over an empty set). For example, if all numbers occur more than once (so no number appears exactly once), Q1 will return a row with NUM = NULL while Q2’s sub‐query may yield no row before the IFNULL is applied.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample that distinguishes the two queries is to load the table only with duplicate values. For instance, insert two copies each of 1 and 2. Then no number appears exactly once. (Q1, by grouping and applying MAX over an empty set, returns a row with NULL; Q2’s sub‐query finds no qualifying row and so may behave differently in some systems.)

q1: SELECT NAME AS CUSTOMERS FROM CUSTOMERS WHERE ID NOT IN (SELECT CUSTOMERID FROM ORDERS)
q2: SELECT NAME AS CUSTOMERS FROM CUSTOMERS WHERE CUSTOMERS.ID != ALL (SELECT CUSTOMERID FROM ORDERS)
q1_mapped: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2_mapped: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE table1.c2 != ALL (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
explanation: The key difference comes from how the two constructs handle a NULL value in the sub‐query. When the sub‐query returns any NULL, the predicate in Q1 (using NOT IN) will yield UNKNOWN (and thus false) for every candidate row, whereas many SQL systems (for example, Oracle) treat the ALL predicate in Q2 in such a way that they compare only the non‐null values. In this counterexample the ORDERS table contains one proper customer id and one NULL value. Then a customer who never actually appears in a non‐null order (e.g. Bob) is rejected by Q1 (because the sub‐query returns NULL) but may be accepted by Q2 (since Bob’s id is not equal to the non‐null ordered id).
counterexample_dsp: We create two customers, 'Alice' (ID 1) and 'Bob' (ID 2). In the ORDERS table we insert one valid order for Alice (customer id 1) and another order row with a NULL customer id. In this situation Q1 returns no rows (since the sub‐query contains NULL, making 'NOT IN' fail for every candidate) while Q2 returns Bob (because Bob’s id is different from the non‐null value 1, and many SQL systems ignore the NULL for the ALL predicate).

explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in that Q1’s self‐join is an inner join (after filtering out equal values) so that if no distinct pair exists then no candidate values are available for MIN(), whereas Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN so that even when no partner row exists for a given X1, a row is produced (with X2 columns as NULL) and then the aggregate is computed over the (non‐empty) result set. In some SQL systems this causes Q1 to yield no row (or a row with NULL) while Q2 always returns one row with NULL. Thus, with a minimal table (a single point) the two queries do not “semantically” behave the same.
counterexample: INSERT INTO POINT (X) VALUES (10);
counterexample_dsp: A test database with only one row in POINT. In this case Q1’s inner join produces no pair (hence no non‐NULL difference values) while Q2’s LEFT JOIN returns one row (with a NULL computed difference). Although both aggregates eventually produce NULL, the intermediate results (and in some implementations even the row count) differ – thereby showing that the two queries are not equivalent.

In a SQL dialect where dividing two integers performs integer division (thus 1/2 yields 0 instead of 0.5), Q1’s expression (SUM/COUNT) may be evaluated as an integer (because the join returns an extra row per player) while Q2’s CTE arithmetic forces a floating–point division. However, Q1 does a simple aggregation over the FOLLOW table (after filtering by those users that occur in the FOLLOWER column), while Q2 uses a self‐join and then counts distinct values. In a “pure set” (duplicate‐free) world they would yield the same counts; but if for any reason duplicate follow–records could occur (that is, if the PK constraint were not enforced or if the relation came from a view that allows duplicates), Q1 would count all duplicate occurrences while Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT …) would eliminate them. (In other words, Q1 “multiplies” duplicates whereas Q2 never does.)

In the test data below the same follow–relationship ('bob','alice') is present twice. (In a real table the PK prevents this, but if you imagine a scenario where duplicates occur, Q1 returns 2 for bob while Q2 returns 1.)

In Q1 the MAX() aggregate is computed over a (possibly empty) derived table and returns one row with a NULL value even when no value appears exactly once. By contrast, Q2 uses a GROUP BY clause so if the table is empty (or if there are no rows at all) it produces no rows at all. q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)

explanation: Q1 is written with 'GROUP BY 1', which in many SQL dialects is interpreted as grouping on the first select‐list expression. However, in some implementations (or with lax ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY settings) it might be misinterpreted as grouping by the constant 1 – thus aggregating the entire CUSTOMER table into one group – whereas Q2 explicitly groups by CUSTOMER_ID so that each customer is processed separately. In our counterexample, when the overall distinct count in the combined group equals the total number of products, Q1 returns a row (with an arbitrarily chosen CUSTOMER_ID), but Q2 does not return any customer because none individually purchased all products.

Although no individual customer bought all products (so Q2 returns nothing), if Q1’s 'GROUP BY 1' is misinterpreted as grouping everything together then the combined distinct count of products is 2 – which equals the total count in PRODUCT – and Q1 returns one row.

    ACTION_DATE DATE,

explanation: At first glance the two queries appear to do the same thing – they filter ACTIONS by REPORT events on 2019‐07‐04, then group by the EXTRA column and count distinct POST_ID values. However, subtle differences in how duplicate rows are handled (in particular, when the underlying ACTIONS table contains duplicate rows, which is allowed since no primary key is defined) can lead to different results. In Q1 the filtering is applied directly to ACTIONS so that duplicate rows (identical in all columns) are simply “folded” by the COUNT(DISTINCT ...) over the already‐filtered set. );
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem equivalent – both are meant to return the buyer‐ids of people having purchased an S8 but never an iPhone. However, they differ in when the S8 filter is applied. In Q1 the join is done and then the WHERE clause immediately restricts to S8 sales, and then excludes any buyer who ever appears in an iPhone sale (via the subquery). In Q2 the join is done over all sales and the NOT IN subquery (which is not correlated) is computed independently; only then is the outer product name filter (P.PRODUCT_NAME = 'S8') applied. This distinction matters when the subquery’s results are “contaminated” by a NULL value. (Recall that if the set produced by the subquery contains even one NULL, then for any candidate value x the test x NOT IN (subquery) evaluates to UNKNOWN rather than TRUE.)  In a data set where an iPhone sale exists with a NULL BUYER_ID, Q1’s subquery (which joins PRODUCT and SALES on the entire table) returns a set that includes NULL. Then, even if a buyer (say, buyer 1) has an S8 sale, the test “buyer 1 NOT IN (…NULL, …)” will fail in Q1 and exclude buyer 1. However, if the data (or the query‐processing engine) arranges the join in Q2 so that the “bad” iPhone row (with a NULL BUYER_ID) is not “visible” to the outer filtering (because the join and filtering order is different), then buyer 1’s S8 row may pass the overall WHERE clause. (Many SQL optimizers treat NOT IN very “cautiously” in the presence of NULLs – but if one is not careful one may get different answers from two seemingly “similar” formulations.)  Hence, these two queries are not semantically equivalent in the face of a “polluted” subquery result from the iPhone join.
counterexample_dsp: We create two products – an S8 and an IPHONE. Then we insert two SALES rows. One records an S8 purchase made by buyer 1. The other is an iPhone sale but with a NULL BUYER_ID. In Q1 the subquery (which returns the buyer IDs from iPhone sales) yields a set containing NULL. Then the condition 1 NOT IN (NULL, …) evaluates to UNKNOWN so buyer 1 is excluded, and Q1 returns no rows. (Depending on the SQL‐engine’s treatment of NULL in NOT IN, Q2 may end up not filtering out buyer 1.) Thus the two queries return different results.

explanation: Q1 and Q2 may seem to enforce the same restriction (“all sales of the product are between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31”), but they do it in different ways. In Q1 the condition is applied over the entire set of a product’s sales (by taking MIN and MAX over all rows), so if even one sale lies outside the period the product is dropped. In Q2 the logic is split into two parts: one CTE grabs product IDs with any sale in the period (CTE1), and the other CTE grabs product IDs with any sale outside the period (CTE2). explanation: The two queries differ when a given player logs in on the same (calendar) day using different devices. In SQL Q1 the IN–subquery is applied directly against the ACTIVITY table so that if a player has more than one row on his earliest EVENT_DATE (for example, if the DATE column only stores the day so that multiple logins on that day appear with the same EVENT_DATE), then Q1 will return every such row (and therefore every DEVICE_ID recorded that day). By contrast, Q2’s WITH–CTE first groups by PLAYER_ID and thereby picks a single minimum EVENT_DATE per player. When that is joined back against ACTIVITY via the tuple comparison, only one copy per player is “guaranteed” (even if there are actually two or more records on that day). q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.X - B.X))) AS SHORTEST FROM POINT AS A, POINT AS B WHERE A.X <> B.X
q2: SELECT MIN(ABS(A.X -B.X) )AS SHORTEST FROM POINT AS A LEFT JOIN POINT AS B ON ABS(A.X-B.X)<=(SELECT MAX(X)-MIN(X) FROM POINT) WHERE A.X != B.X

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be doing the same thing—computing the least absolute difference (among pairs of distinct points) from the POINT table. In fact, if you look at any set of two or more numbers (all lying between the minimum and the maximum), every difference |a – b| is necessarily ≤ (MAX(X) – MIN(X)), so the ON‐clause in Q2 is never the source of a missing pair. However, the two queries differ in how they treat the “edge case” when there is only one row in POINT. In Q1 the FROM clause (a cross–product filtered by A.X <> B.X) produces no rows (so MIN is computed over an empty set, yielding NULL), while in Q2 the LEFT JOIN always retains the row from A even though the only possible join candidate (B, namely the same row) is later rejected by the WHERE clause. (Note that many SQL engines will then return a single row with MIN(ABS(...)) = NULL even though a “no‐result” condition is signaled – but conceptually the two queries are not “semantically equivalent” because Q2 guarantees one output row while Q1 yields no rows before aggregation in the absence of at least two distinct points.)  To force a visible difference in application code (for example, when the client distinguishes “no row returned” from “one row with a NULL value”), one may use a test database that has exactly one point.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.X - B.X))) AS SHORTEST FROM POINT AS A, POINT AS B WHERE A.X <> B.X
q2: SELECT MIN(ABS(X1.X - X2.X)) AS SHORTEST FROM POINT X1 JOIN POINT X2 WHERE X1.X != X2.X

explanation: The subtle difference is how the join is performed. In Q1 the FROM clause uses an explicit Cartesian product of POINT as A and POINT as B (with the condition A.X <> B.X filtering out self-pairs), so every distinct pair of rows is considered. In Q2 the use of 'JOIN' without an explicit ON clause is interpreted (in many SQL engines) as a NATURAL JOIN. Since the table POINT has only one column (X), the NATURAL JOIN automatically joins on X; that is, it only pairs rows where X1.X = X2.X. Then the WHERE clause (X1.X != X2.X) removes all rows. Thus, for a table with two distinct values Q1 produces a result (the actual minimum difference) while Q2 produces no rows (or a NULL result).

INSERT INTO POINT (X) VALUES (2);
counterexample_dsp: By inserting two points with distinct X values (eg, 1 and 2) we force Q1 to compute the absolute difference between 1 and 2 (which is 1) while Q2, after performing a NATURAL JOIN on X, yields no join pairs (and hence returns NULL or no row).
