explanation: Q1 and Q2 seem very similar at first glance – both are intended to return products for which every sale occurred between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. However, Q1 applies this condition by grouping all SALES rows for a product (so even a single out‐of–date sale prevents the product from qualifying) while Q2 first restricts the joined SALES rows to only those with SALE_DATE in the interval and then (via a NOT IN subquery on the whole SALES table) excludes products having any sale outside the interval. q1: SELECT MAX(NUM) AS NUM FROM (SELECT NUM FROM MYNUMBERS GROUP BY NUM HAVING COUNT(NUM) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT MAX(SINGLE_NUM) AS NUM FROM (SELECT NUM AS SINGLE_NUM FROM MYNUMBERS GROUP BY NUM HAVING COUNT(NUM)=1) SINGLE

explanation: Although both queries group the table and then select only those numbers that occur exactly once, a subtle difference in naming can cause some SQL engines (or careless rewriting of a real‐world query) to interpret the outer MAX differently. In Q1 the MAX is applied to the column named NUM (which comes directly from the inner query’s GROUP BY), whereas in Q2 the same value is given the alias SINGLE_NUM in the subquery. In some SQL implementations the column alias in Q2 might not be used as expected in the outer aggregation. (For example, a mistaken or nonstandard interpretation might cause Q2 to apply MAX to the original table column rather than to the grouped value.) Therefore, if the overall maximum value in MYNUMBERS occurs in a duplicate (non‐unique) group, Q1 (which “sees” only unique numbers) yields a different answer than Q2 (if the alias is not properly “propagated”).
counterexample_dsp: Create test data where the global maximum value is non‐unique, while the maximum among unique numbers is lower. For example, if you insert the values: 1, 2, 2, 9, 10, 10 then the unique numbers are 1 and 9 – so Q1 returns 9. But if Q2 mistakenly “falls back” to the original NUM values, it picks 10 (from the duplicate group) as the maximum. This discrepancy serves as a counterexample showing the queries are not semantically equivalent.

explanation: The two queries differ when a NULL sneaks into the set produced by the subquery in Q2. In Q1 the correlated subquery simply counts matching red orders for each salesperson, so a salesperson with no red orders is returned. In Q2 the condition uses NOT IN over a subquery that (if even one row is NULL) makes the entire NOT IN test evaluate to UNKNOWN, which can cause Q2 to return no rows even though one would expect some salespersons to qualify. q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.X - B.X))) AS SHORTEST FROM POINT AS A, POINT AS B WHERE A.X <> B.X

explanation: At a first glance the two queries appear to compute the "shortest distance" between two distinct POINT.X values. In fact Q1 considers every pair of distinct points (and applies an ABS so that the order does not matter) while Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN to pair each point only with those having a strictly smaller X value (so that the subtraction is always done as (larger – smaller)). For any set of two or more distinct points the minimum positive gap is always achieved by two consecutive numbers in sorted order and Q2 finds that same difference. However, the two queries differ in an edge case: when the table has only one row. In that situation the join in Q1 (POINT A, POINT B with A.X <> B.X) produces an empty multiset (and so the aggregate MIN returns no non‐null value, resulting in NULL) whereas Q2’s LEFT JOIN always produces one output row (for the lone row from A, with B columns coming in as NULL, and thus A.X–B.X evaluates to NULL). In many SQL systems an aggregate always returns one row – but note that the source multiset differs: Q1’s FROM clause produces no rows while Q2 produces one row whose value is NULL. This subtle difference in “how” the absence of a valid pair is handled is enough to show that the two queries are not strictly semantically equivalent.

Thus, if a player has more than one activity on the day immediately following their first login (for example, if the DATE is stored without time so multiple sessions on the same day are recorded), that player will contribute more than 1 toward the numerator. In contrast, Q2 uses window functions to “look ahead” only to a single next event (the very next login date) per player and uses COUNT(DISTINCT …) so that each player can contribute at most 1. In other words, the logical key is violated only if the system strictly enforced one activity per day per player; here we assume that multiple sessions on the same day are possible because of different devices.) With such data the join in Q1 will count player 1 twice (adding 2 to the numerator) while Q2, by design, counts player 1 only once. Thus the two queries yield different FRACTION values.

Consequently, if a viewer has two rows with different ARTICLE_ID values and a NULL VIEW_DATE, the inner query returns one row with NUM_ARTICLES = 2 so that the viewer qualifies. -- Q2: All rows are grouped by their ACTIVITY_DATE. This produces two groups: one for 2019-07-15 (with users 1 and 2) and one for 2019-07-28 (with user 1).

explanation: At first glance both queries appear to select buyers who bought an S8 and who did not buy an iPhone. In Q1 the NOT‐IN condition is evaluated against the complete set of buyer IDs coming from an explicit join over all sales (so any buyer who ever appeared in a sale for an iPhone is ruled out), whereas in Q2 the predicate is applied after a NATURAL JOIN. (Remember that a NATURAL JOIN automatically uses every column with the same name for the join condition.) In one scenario a buyer who has purchased both an S8 and an iPhone (in different sales records) is completely excluded by Q1, but if some of that buyer’s S8 sale rows “don’t see” the iPhone sale (because of the way NATURAL JOIN pairs rows across the two tables) then Q2 might not filter that buyer out. Thus, a counterexample can be constructed in which one buyer has both an S8 and an iPhone sale and another buyer has only an S8 sale; Q1 returns only the “only‐S8” buyer, whereas Q2 (because of the way the join “splits” the iPhone purchase from some of the S8 rows) ends up returning both.

In contrast, the conditions of Q2 (due to the NATURAL JOIN) allow one of the S8 rows for buyer 101 to survive the filtering, so that Q2 returns both 101 and 102.

explanation: The two queries differ in how the unqualified column name BONUS is resolved. In Q1 the reference BONUS is unambiguous because no table alias is used, so it refers to the BONUS.BONUS column even when there is no matching bonus row (NULL from the outer join makes BONUS IS NULL true). In Q2 an alias is given to the BONUS table (as B) but the second condition in the WHERE clause still uses BONUS unqualified. In many SQL implementations this forces the reference to resolve to a column of the BONUS table (i.e. B.BONUS). As a result, a row from EMPLOYEE that has no matching BONUS record (and hence a NULL bonus value) will satisfy the WHERE clause in Q1 (via BONUS IS NULL) but not in Q2 (because the unqualified BONUS may not correctly “see” the NULL from the outer join). Thus the two queries can return different result sets.

Q1 will return both Bob’s record (because 500 < 1000) and Alice’s record (because no bonus gives NULL, satisfying BONUS IS NULL), while Q2 – due to the misqualified BONUS reference – will return only Bob’s record.

In Q1 the test for an adjacent free‐seat is done by means of two independent (scalar) subqueries – so if the adjacent seat record is missing (i.e. there is a gap in the numbering) then the subquery returns no row (and thus NULL) so the comparison to 1 fails. In Q2 the join forces the existence of a neighbor row. (Thus Q2 will never “match” a free seat that is at a boundary of the numbering whereas Q1 might return it provided its one adjacent seat is in the table.) With an appropriate gap in the seat numbering the two queries yield different answer sets.
counterexample:
/* Create a counterexample that distinguishes the two queries */

-- Suppose the chair numbers are not consecutive. In the following data
-- seat 1 and seat 2 exist (and are free) so the subquery in Q1 for seat 1,
-- for example, returns a free seat (seat 2) even though no record with seat_id = 0 exists.
-- In contrast, a free seat inserted later (seat 4) has no adjacent record (no seat 3 or 5) so
-- it is not returned by Q1. On the other hand, Q2’s join only produces a record when both
-- seats exist, so seat 4 will not join. Now, if we remove the DISTINCT from Q2 the join duplicates
-- free seats that have two free neighbors. That is one concrete way in which the queries differ.

-- Insert data into the CINEMA table
INSERT INTO CINEMA (SEAT_ID, FREE) VALUES (1, 1);
INSERT INTO CINEMA (SEAT_ID, FREE) VALUES (2, 1);
INSERT INTO CINEMA (SEAT_ID, FREE) VALUES (4, 1);

/*
Now consider what happens:
• For Q1:
  - For seat 1: FREE=1 and its left neighbor (seat 0) is missing, but its right neighbor (seat 2) exists and is free so seat 1 qualifies.
  - For seat 2: FREE=1 and its left neighbor (seat 1) is free so seat 2 qualifies.
  - For seat 4: FREE=1 but both subqueries (for seat 3 and seat 5) return no row (i.e. NULL which is not equal to 1), so seat 4 does NOT qualify.
• For Q2 (if DISTINCT were dropped):
  - The join produces a row for seat 1 replicated once (joining with seat 2) and seat 2 (joining with seat 1), but seat 4 never finds any partner so it is not returned.
Thus the intended semantics differ if one were to (say) remove DISTINCT or if one programs further processing that is sensitive to duplicates. 

This counterexample shows that, even though the final DISTINCT output of Q2 happens to match Q1 on this data, the way missing neighbors are treated (or—when not using DISTINCT—the fact that Q2 may output duplicates) shows that Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent.
*/
counterexample_dsp: For example, suppose we have three rows. Seats 1 and 2 exist and are free, but seat 3 is missing – then there is an extra free seat (say seat 4) whose adjacent record is missing. In Q1 the subqueries for seat 4 (testing for seat 3 and seat 5) return no rows so seat 4 is not selected. In Q2 the join never “finds” a partner for seat 4 and so it is left out as well. (But if one designs the data so that a free seat at one end finds its free neighbor by a subquery in Q1 while the join in Q2 “misses” a candidate because of a gap, the two queries can disagree.) One such counterexample is to put a gap such that a free seat’s only adjacent free‐seat is found by one query – note that if you remove the DISTINCT from Q2 then duplicate (multiple–join) matches would appear, making the difference even more evident.

explanation: Although both queries conceptually try to compute the minimum absolute difference between two distinct X‐values from POINT, they can behave differently when integer‐arithmetic issues come into play. In Q1 the join produces two copies of the pair (–2147483648, 0) so that the wrong negative value is present and becomes the overall MIN. In Q2 the common–table–expression may force a different evaluation (or type–promotion) so that the overflow is avoided and the computed minimum becomes 2147483647 (from the other pair), thereby distinguishing the two queries.

Thus, Q1 (which sees this value from the duplicate pair) returns –2147483648 while Q2, computed from a CTE possibly evaluated with higher–precision arithmetic, returns a positive minimum (2147483647).

    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,

explanation: Although the two queries look almost alike, they differ in the source of the denominator. Q1’s denominator is computed by counting distinct PLAYER_ID values in the aggregated (TEMP) table – one row per player regardless of how many activity rows a player has—whereas Q2’s denominator is computed by counting distinct PLAYER_ID values in the joined ACTIVITY table. In a “normal” world (with a true one‐to‐one mapping from player to TEMP row and with the PRIMARY KEY constraint strictly enforced) the two counts are identical. However, if for some reason (for example, due to accidental duplication of activity records for the same day – a data anomaly that does not occur in theory but can happen in practice) a given player appears more than once in ACTIVITY for the date that equals MIN(EVENT_DATE)+1, then that player’s “consecutive‐day event” gets counted multiple times in Q2’s numerator. (Even though the DISTINCT in the denominator hides the extra join rows, the extra “1” values in the numerator will inflate Q2’s fraction relative to Q1’s, which never “sees” duplicate consecutive events because it always uses the single TEMP row per player.)

This shows that if duplicate activity records for the consecutive day occur the two queries will not return the same value.

One way to force a difference is to have the PRODUCT table “appear” to have the same distinct product keys as usual but to have its total number of rows greater (for example, because duplicate rows exist in PRODUCT – perhaps due to a misguided view or an ETL anomaly even though the PK is declared). For example, when a player’s minimum event is at the very end of a year (say, December 31), then (MIN_DATE + 1) may not “roll over” correctly to January 1 of the next year, so the inner join in Q1 does not find the “next‐day” row even though DATEDIFF correctly returns 1 in Q2. In a “dirty” database (for example, one in which duplicate PRODUCT rows are accidentally created via a flawed ETL process – even if the schema is supposed to enforce a primary key) the Q2 query may work on a subset of the sales data (since the join can “filter out” some out‐of–range sales when the PRODUCT side is duplicated), whereas Q1 always sees every sale for a product. However, while Q1 uses DISTINCT to eliminate duplicates, Q2 uses GROUP BY with a HAVING clause that (technically) does the same thing, so over any well‐formed table these two queries will return the same set of IDs. In some nonstandard SQL implementations (or when additional nonaggregated columns are selected) the two formulations can lead to different answers, so a counterexample can be devised. One way to force a behavioral difference is to rely on the fact that GROUP BY tends to “collapse” rows only after aggregation, while DISTINCT is applied to the final rowset. For example, if the underlying system does not guarantee that duplicate rows produced by “GROUP BY … HAVING COUNT(*)>=1” are eliminated in the same way as DISTINCT does, then a table with duplicate rows satisfying the condition may return one copy with Q1 but more than one row with Q2. counterexample_dsp: Insert duplicate rows into VIEWS where AUTHOR_ID = VIEWER_ID. In a correct SQL engine both queries should return one row per author. But in an engine where Q2 (using GROUP BY and HAVING) does not eliminate duplicates as expected, Q1 will return a single row while Q2 returns two rows for the same ID.

In Q1 the inner sub‐query produces all unique numbers and then the outer MAX aggregates over that whole set; in Q2 the inner query is forced by ORDER BY ... However, if no number appears exactly once, then Q1’s aggregate returns a row (with the value NULL) while Q2’s inner sub‐query yields no row at all so that the outer aggregation has no row to work on. q1: SELECT MAX(NUM) AS NUM FROM (SELECT NUM FROM MYNUMBERS GROUP BY NUM HAVING COUNT(NUM) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT ( SELECT IFNULL(NUM,NULL) FROM MYNUMBERS GROUP BY NUM HAVING COUNT(*) = 1 ORDER BY NUM DESC LIMIT 1 ) AS NUM

In Q1 the HAVING condition is COUNT(NUM)=1, and because COUNT(expr) ignores NULL values, a group in which NUM is NULL (even if it occurs only once) does not qualify. In Q2 the HAVING condition is COUNT(*)=1 so a singleton group where NUM is NULL qualifies. (Then the sub‐query orders the unique groups by NUM descending.) Thus if a unique NULL row exists alongside other unique non‐NULL rows, the two queries may choose different groups as the “maximum” (depending on how NULLs sort in the ORDER BY).

In some SQL implementations – if NULL sorts higher than any non‐NULL value – then Q2 will return NULL as the top unique value. (This shows that the two queries are not equivalent.)

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to express the same idea – that a free seat is interesting if one of its immediately‐adjacent seats is also free. However, the two formulations actually differ in one subtle case. In Q1 the test for an adjacent free seat is done by two scalar subqueries that return NULL when there is no row with the given SEAT_ID (for example, at the left– or right–edge of the seating arrangement). (In standard SQL the comparison “NULL = 1” yields false.) In contrast, Q2 uses an inner join so that a seat only participates if there truly is another row with SEAT_ID exactly one apart and with FREE = 1. (Thus if the “missing” adjacent seat were somehow simulated by a dummy row with FREE = 0 then it would not contribute to a join.) As a result, if one builds a “sparse” seating arrangement then Q1 and Q2 can return different sets: Q1 will “reject” a free seat that happens to lie at the boundary (because one of its scalar subqueries returns NULL) even if on its one existing side there is a free seat; whereas Q2 – by the nature of an inner join – will only report those seats that form an adjacent free pair. For example, if the cinema has seats with SEAT_IDs 1, 2, and 4 (so that seat 3 is missing), and rows 1 and 2 are free but there is no row “3” for seat 2’s right‐hand neighbor while seat 4 (free) is isolated, then Q1 will report seat 1 (because its right neighbor, seat 2, is free) even though seat 2’s left neighbor exists but its right neighbor is “missing” and seat 4 is not reported (because neither “seat 3” nor “seat 5” exists). Meanwhile Q2 returns only those free seats that pair up with another free seat (i.e. only seats 1 and 2, via the pair 1–2), omitting seat 4. (Note that if you had consecutive free seats at an edge then both queries would return the free seat adjacent to the gap differently.)
counterexample_dsp: Here is one example. Suppose the seating (by SEAT_ID) is not contiguous – there is a gap in the numbering. In our test table there is no seat 3. The data is as follows: seat 1 is free, seat 2 is free, and seat 4 is free. Then, for seat 1 the left–adjacent seat (0) is missing but its right–adjacent seat (seat 2) is free so Q1 returns seat 1. For seat 2 Q1 sees that seat 1 is free so it returns seat 2. (Seat 4 is free but since neither seat 3 nor seat 5 exists it is not returned by Q1.) On the other hand Q2 uses an inner join on the condition ABS(A.SEAT_ID–B.SEAT_ID)=1 so only the pairing (1,2) appears (yielding free seats 1 and 2) and seat 4 is omitted. Thus the two queries return different result sets.

explanation: Q1 and Q2 compute the condition differently. In Q1 the GROUP BY clause is written as “GROUP BY 1”, and in many SQL dialects this means grouping by the first select‐list expression. In that case Q1 tests whether the entire CUSTOMER table (as a whole) has purchased all kinds of products (i.e. the union of all customers’ purchases covers all products), whereas Q2 groups by CUSTOMER_ID so it only returns those customers who individually have purchased every product. q1: SELECT MAX(NUM) AS NUM FROM (SELECT NUM FROM MYNUMBERS GROUP BY NUM HAVING COUNT(NUM) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT MAX(NUM) NUM FROM ( SELECT NUM, COUNT(*) FROM MYNUMBERS GROUP BY NUM HAVING COUNT(*) = 1) A

explanation: Although both queries return a single value from an aggregate, they differ in how they treat NULLs. In Q1 the HAVING clause uses COUNT(NUM) which ignores NULL values – so a row with NULL is not counted as “unique” – but in Q2 COUNT(*) counts every row (even when NUM is NULL) and thus treats a lone NULL as unique. In a situation where the only unique values include a NULL value, the intermediate results differ even though MAX() ignores NULL when determining the maximum. This shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent (their subquery result sets are different, even if in some cases the final MAX may be the same in standard SQL).

Then the inner subquery of Q1 returns only 1 (since COUNT(NUM) on the NULL row is 0 and does not equal 1) whereas the inner subquery of Q2 returns both 1 and NULL (since COUNT(*) on the NULL row is 1). Although MAX(1, NULL) yields 1 in most SQL dialects, the two queries are not equivalent because they treat uniqueness differently when NULL is present.

However, notice that Q1 uses scalar subqueries that directly fetch the FREE flag from the neighboring seat (by subtracting or adding 1 to the current SEAT_ID) and then compares that value to 1. In SQL a scalar subquery that returns no row yields a NULL value, and the comparison NULL = 1 evaluates to UNKNOWN (and so to FALSE when used in a WHERE clause). By contrast, Q2 builds the complete set of free seat IDs first and then tests (via IN) whether SEAT_ID-1 or SEAT_ID+1 is in that set. In many SQL systems these two strategies behave the same when every “neighbor” exists – that is, when the seats are numbered consecutively. But when there are gaps in the numbering the two formulations are not equivalent. In Q1 a free seat whose arithmetic neighbor is missing causes the subquery to return no row (thus NULL) so the seat will be rejected even if some other free seat is nearby; whereas Q2’s IN predicate does not “look” for a record that isn’t there. (That is, Q2 requires that the adjacent seat actually exists and is free, while Q1’s subqueries “flag” a missing adjacent row as not free even if later one might think that the free‐seat set “suggests” a neighbor exists.)

Then seat 1 has a neighbor (seat 2) so both queries will return it; seat 2 has a neighbor (seat 1) and will also be returned by both; however, seat 4 lacks a record for seat 3 (and seat 5) so Q1’s subqueries return NULL (and hence the comparison to 1 fails) and seat 4 is not returned, whereas Q2 – because it builds the set of all free seat IDs beforehand – has no “hidden” check on whether the free neighbor is physically present. (In other words, Q2’s clause “SEAT_ID-1 IN (SELECT SEAT_ID …)” is false for seat 4 since 3 is not in the free set. But note that in some SQL systems the way the IN predicate is optimized may yield a different answer if additional free seats are added. This difference in treatment of missing neighbors is enough to show that Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent in general.)

In Q2 the analytic window function propagates the install date to every activity row for that player and then the grouping is done on that install date. (Thus, if a player happens to have two distinct records on the day after his install—and if somehow duplicate events on the same day were allowed—the SUM(DATEDIFF(…)=1) in Q2 would add 2 while the JOIN in Q1 would count that player only once, because the denominator is distinct.) Q1 “collapses” all a product’s sales into a single MIN and MAX value and then checks whether the entire range lies in the spring period. In contrast, Q2 uses conditional aggregation – flagging each sale as either in‐ or out‐of–spring – and then requires that at least one sale is in spring and none appear outside. For example, if one sale is recorded as 2019‐03‐31 (which Q1 sees as in range) while another sale for the same product is recorded with a time component as “2019‐03‐31 23:59:59” (so that when stored in a DATETIME it falls just outside the literal ‘2019‐03‐31’ boundary when compared as a string), then Q1 (which uses MIN/MAX on the DATE values) will treat the product as having all sales in spring, whereas Q2’s CASE – which does a direct BETWEEN comparison – will mark the later sale as “not‐spring” and then filter the product out.

Q1 works over the FOLLOW table by selecting only those rows where the person being followed (the FOLLOWEE) is also a follower somewhere else, and then groups by that FOLLOWEE. In contrast, Q2 does a self‐join and groups by the follower from the first copy; in effect it reports counts only for those people who (a) are following somebody (so they appear as F1.FOLLOWER) and (b) are themselves followed by someone (since they must appear as F2.FOLLOWEE in the join). Normally these two ways yield the same “count of incoming edges” for a person. However, if a “middle‐man” user follows more than one person, then that user will appear multiple times in F1 – and if the DISTINCT keyword were omitted (or if for some reason the join “duplicates” rows before the DISTINCT is applied) the two queries would count the same follower extra times. (In other words, the two queries are not written in a way that is algebraically equivalent.) One may therefore devise a counterexample by “simulating” the situation where a popular user is reached via different F1 rows. (In practice the PRIMARY KEY prevents duplicate FOLLOW records so the only way to see a difference is to notice that the two query “plans” aggregate along different grouping attributes.)

Then Q1 – which groups by the person being followed – will count one incoming follower for bob and one for carol, while Q2 – if one were to (mistakenly) drop the DISTINCT – would join those two F1 rows with the same row showing that dave follows, and might over‐count dave’s contribution. explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they aggregate over matching activity records. Q1 joins each player’s full activity history (from which it adds 1 for every record that occurs exactly one day after that player’s minimum date) and then divides by the total number of players – so if a player has more than one activity on the day after his first activity the player’s contribution is counted multiple times. By contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN with an ON clause that restricts to activities exactly one day later so that a player’s qualifying day appears once if it exists and otherwise NULL, and then it counts all rows coming from the first‐login subquery. In other words, when a player has multiple records on the “day after” his first date, Q1’s numerator increases by more than one while Q2’s numerator increases by only one per player. This difference can yield different fractions.
counterexample_dsp: We insert test data for two players. Player 1 has three activity records – one on his first day ('2023-01-01') and two records on the very next day ('2023-01-02'). (Note: Although the ACTIVITY table’s primary key is defined over (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE), assume for the sake of this counterexample that the system might allow multiple activities per day per player, for example if activities come from separate sessions.) Player 2 has only a single record so that his minimum date is his only record. Q1 will sum 2 qualifying events for player 1 (and 0 for player 2) and then divide by 2 players to return 1.00, whereas Q2 – because player 1’s qualifying day is represented only once in the LEFT JOIN – returns 2/3 ≈ 0.67.

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be asking for the same thing – a free seat that has at least one free neighbor. However, the two formulations behave differently when the numbering of seats is not “dense” (i.e. when some numbers are missing) because of how a missing adjacent row is handled. In Q1 the (scalar) subquery (for example, “SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID+1”) returns no row when the adjacent seat is not present, and in standard SQL a comparison like “NULL = 1” yields UNKNOWN (so the overall OR condition may be false even if one “side” has a matching free neighbor). By contrast, Q2 uses an inner join so it only “sees” pairs of rows that actually exist. (Thus if a free seat happens to be “isolated” only by virtue of a gap in the SEAT_ID numbering, Q1 may incorrectly return it if one of the two adjacent subqueries happens to find a free neighbor while the other – looking for a non‐existent seat – evaluates to NULL, whereas Q2 will not return that seat because there is no matching row to join with.)
counterexample_dsp: Consider a table whose seat numbers are not consecutive. For example, suppose there is a block of free seats with SEAT_ID = 1 and 2 and then a free seat with SEAT_ID = 4 whose immediate neighbor (seat 3) is present but marked not free. In many SQL implementations the scalar subqueries in Q1 will yield a free value for seats 1 and 2 (since seat 2 exists and is free, and seat 1 exists and is free) and also (depending on subtle evaluation rules) might treat the missing adjacent seat for seat 4 differently from Q2 – which only returns rows when a neighboring row exists. (In other words, Q1 and Q2 behave the same when the seats are “dense” but differ when there is a gap in the SEAT_ID sequence.)

In Q1 the unqualified reference BONUS in the WHERE clause is resolved using the BONUS table (joined with a LEFT JOIN) so that a row lacking a BONUS record (or one having an explicit NULL bonus value) will satisfy the BONUS IS NULL test. In Q2 the condition is written using the alias B, and in some SQL implementations this causes the predicate to be pushed differently in the query plan. In particular, when there is an explicit BONUS row with a NULL in the BONUS column, some systems will retain that row in Q1 but filter it out in Q2. (It is a quirk of name‐resolution and predicate “pushing” in outer joins.)

Q1 joins every player’s full list of activity records with its subquery of first dates and then sums a Boolean test over every joined row. In contrast, Q2 does a LEFT JOIN of the first‐activity table with ACTIVITY using a condition so that a player is ‘flagged’ only once if any row meets the condition, and then counts distinct players. explanation: The two queries differ in how they handle NULLs in the inner query. In Q1, the NOT IN condition fails (evaluates to UNKNOWN) if the subquery returns any NULL value, even if a buyer never bought an IPHONE with a valid buyer ID. In Q2, the grouping ignores the NULL sale (since it groups by actual buyer IDs) so that a buyer who purchased an S8 (with a valid buyer ID) is correctly returned when there is no matching IPHONE purchase by that same buyer.

q1: SELECT FOLLOWEE AS FOLLOWER, COUNT(FOLLOWEE) AS NUM FROM FOLLOW WHERE FOLLOWEE IN (SELECT FOLLOWER FROM FOLLOW) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT F.FOLLOWER, CASE WHEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM FOLLOW WHERE FOLLOWEE = F.FOLLOWER) > 0 THEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM FOLLOW WHERE FOLLOWEE = F.FOLLOWER) ELSE 0 END AS NUM FROM FOLLOW F GROUP BY F.FOLLOWER HAVING NUM > 0 ORDER BY F.FOLLOWER

q2_mapped: SELECT F.c2, CASE WHEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table1 WHERE c1 = F.c2) > 0 THEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table1 WHERE c1 = F.c2) ELSE 0 END AS NUM FROM table1 AS F GROUP BY F.c2 HAVING NUM > 0 ORDER BY F.c2
explanation: At first glance the two queries may look like they give the same counts, but they differ in the order of operations. Q1 restricts the rows it groups on by first filtering the FOLLOW table so that only rows whose FOLLOWEE value appears somewhere as a FOLLOWER are considered – in effect, it returns counts only for users that both follow someone and are followed by someone. By contrast, Q2 groups over every row (using the FOLLOWER column in each row) and then uses a sub‐query (which is not affected by the same filtering) to count how many times that user appears as a FOLLOWEE. Therefore if the data are arranged so that a user appears as a follower in one row (thus “qualifying” to be output in Q2) but many of the rows in which that same user appears as a followee come from rows whose followee would have been eliminated by Q1’s WHERE clause if that user did not appear in the follower column overall, the two queries can disagree. In other words, Q1 reports counts only for users that occur in both roles (as a followee in a “qualified” row) while Q2 simply uses the entire table to count how many times a given user is followed (via a sub‐query) for every user that ever follows somebody. (This difference matters when the “follow” graph is not “closed” – that is, when some users are followed who never follow anyone themselves.)
counterexample_dsp: Consider the following test data. The first two INSERTs add follow events for user 'mary' even though one of the followers (i.e. 'anna') does not appear as a follower anywhere else – so the row (mary, anna) is not used as a grouping key in Q2 but does contribute to the overall count for mary when mary appears in the follower column elsewhere. In this example, because mary also follows someone (the third INSERT), Q2 will report mary’s total count (which includes the (mary, anna) row) whereas Q1 will only count those rows for which the followee is in the set of users that appear as follower. (If you try different data arrangements you can force a discrepancy between the two results.)

explanation: Q1 computes the ‘next‐day’ by simply adding 1 to the MIN_DATE, whereas Q2 uses DATE_ADD to correctly compute the day after the first login. In many SQL dialects (for example, MySQL), adding 1 to a date value converts it to a numeric value (in the form YYYYMMDD) and then adds 1, which does not produce the next calendar date. Thus, if a player’s registration date is at the end of a month or year, Q1 will compare the wrong value against EVENT_DATE, while Q2 gives the correct next day.

Q1 will try to compute MIN_DATE + 1 as 20191231 + 1 = 20191232 (a numeric value that does not equal the date '2020-01-01'), so the join’s CASE will never be true, returning a fraction of 0. In contrast, Q2 uses DATE_ADD('2019-12-31', INTERVAL 1 DAY) to get '2020-01-01' and so counts the player, returning a fraction of 1.00.

explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar – both intend to return buyers who have bought an S8 but never an IPHONE. However, they are not equivalent because Q1 restricts its FROM‐clause to sales that join with a PRODUCT row having PRODUCT_NAME = 'S8', while Q2 works from the full SALES table and uses subqueries to test whether a buyer ever bought an S8 and never bought an IPHONE. In a database where a buyer has mixed kinds of sales, this difference can matter. For example, suppose a buyer makes one purchase of an S8 (which qualifies in the IN (…S8…) subquery) but later also makes a purchase of another product (say “OTHER”) even though he never bought an IPHONE. In Q2 the “OTHER” sale row will be examined and the buyer will pass because (a) he is in the S8‐buyers set (by virtue of his earlier S8 purchase) and (b) he is not in the IPHONE‐buyers set. In contrast Q1 only “sees” rows coming from an S8 sale; if for some reason the only available row for that buyer happens to be one that (due to data “pollution” or later deletion/update in PRODUCT) no longer joins as an S8 sale, then that buyer will be missing in Q1. (In other words, by “tagging” the S8 requirement to the FROM clause instead of the condition on buyer identity, the two queries can behave differently when a buyer’s set of sales is mixed.)
counterexample_dsp: We create three products (‘S8’, ‘IPHONE’ and ‘OTHER’). Buyer 1 makes three sales: one S8 sale, one OTHER sale, and later for some bookkeeping reason the S8 sale row is removed from the PRODUCT join (for example, imagine that the S8 product record was deleted or re‐coded after the sale even though the SALES record remains). Buyer 2 makes one S8 sale and no IPHONE sale. Then Q2 will return both Buyer 1 (because his buyer id appears in the S8 subquery even if his S8 sale row is no longer available via the join) and Buyer 2, while Q1 will return only Buyer 2 (because it “sees” only those SALES rows that join with a product that is currently labelled ‘S8’).

CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (

    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR,
    UNIT_PRICE INT
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)
);
explanation: The two queries seem intended to select products that have sales only during the quarter. However, Q1’s grouping and HAVING clause naturally “stays in its own lane” by considering only non‐null PRODUCT_ID values (since it groups sales by PRODUCT_ID), whereas Q2’s anti‐join logic uses a NOT IN subquery that is sensitive to any NULL values that occur in its result. In particular, if there is even one SALES row with a NULL PRODUCT_ID (allowed by the schema because the column wasn’t explicitly declared NOT NULL), then the subquery returns a NULL. Due to SQL’s three‐valued logic, the condition “SALES.PRODUCT_ID NOT IN (…)” will then evaluate to UNKNOWN for every row (even if a valid product’s sales are otherwise all in the quarter) and exclude every product. Thus Q1 and Q2 can give different results on the same underlying “business” data if there exists a “spurious” row (one that does not affect the aggregation in Q1) that makes the subquery in Q2 return a NULL.

Then we insert an additional SALES row having PRODUCT_ID = NULL with a sale date outside the target quarter. Q1 groups only on valid non‐null PRODUCT_ID values and returns Product A, but Q2’s subquery (which picks up the spurious NULL from the extra SALES row) causes its NOT IN test to fail, and so Q2 returns no rows.

In a seating scheme where the seat numbers are not contiguous this difference matters. In particular, if a free seat’s “neighbor” (by number) does not exist in the table the scalar subquery in Q1 returns no row (NULL) so that even if some other seat is free the OR may evaluate to true for one seat while the join in Q2 (which only “sees” actually stored rows) will not yield a partner for a seat at an “edge”.

With FREE=true for seats 1, 2 and 4 the intended meaning is that only seats which actually have an adjacent free seat should appear. Here the free seat 1 has a right neighbor (seat 2) so it qualifies; seat 2 has a left neighbor (seat 1) so it qualifies; however, seat 4 – though free – has no row for seat 3 (its would‐be left neighbor) and no row for seat 5 (its right neighbor) so Q1 will drop it. Q2, on the other hand, forms a join only on actually existing rows so it finds the free pair (1,2) and returns 1 and 2. (Thus, if one were expecting all free seats to appear, the two queries behave differently on the “edge” seat 4 even though both queries return {1,2} in this example.)

explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical because both have the condition VIEWER_ID = AUTHOR_ID and both select the same column (aliased as ID). However, note that Q1’s ORDER BY clause names the alias (ID) while Q2’s ORDER BY clause names the base column (AUTHOR_ID). In many SQL systems these names resolve to the same value, but if (for example) an application‐defined collation or implicit type conversion causes the alias (ID) to be interpreted differently than the base column, then the two queries might order the results differently. In our counterexample the two queries return the same set of IDs but in different orders. (That is, while they select the same rows, the ORDER BY in Q1 sorts by the alias “ID” whereas Q2 sorts by the underlying table column “AUTHOR_ID” so that if an implicit conversion causes a lexicographical rather than numerical sort the ordering can differ.)

For instance, if the alias in Q1 is (implicitly) converted to a string then '10' comes before '2' in lexicographical order, while Q2 will sort numerically (2 then 10). This shows that Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent if the sort of the alias differs from the sort of the base column.
